subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND INDEBTEDNESS, AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES

speechtext:
Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of National Revenue-for the Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to authorize the Canadian National Railway Company to issue securities not exceeding $17,574,233 in principal amount to provide the moneys necessary to meet expenditures made and indebtedness incurred by the companies or railways comprised in the National Railway system during the calendar year 1938; to authorize the governor in council to guarantee the principal, interest and sinking funds of such securities; and to authorize the making of temporary loans to the said company secured

speechtext:

(a)	Retirement of maturing capital obligations, miscellaneous matured or unmatured notes and other obligations, secured or unsecured, and payment of sinking fund not exceeding $9,019,233; and
(b)	Additions and betterments, including coordinations and acquisition of real or personal property not exceeding $8,555,000, estimated as follows:
General additions and betterments, $12,321,392.
Less equipment retirements, $7,921,392.
That leaves a balance of $4,400,000 as the sum that is required for general additions and betterments,. The general additions and betterments for the year 1938 that will be paid for out of capital will be $4,400,000.
In addition, there are new equipment purchases, amounting to $3,455,000. This sum is only one-quarter of the new equipment purchases that will be made during the year 1938, but the railway company itself has power under legislation passed some years ago to purchase or issue notes for raising money for the payment of three-quarters of the sum required for new equipment purchases. This house has to vote the other quarter, which amounts to $3,455,000.
The remaining item is $700,000 for the acquisition of securities. Those are the securities of three companies, the shares of which are owned by the Canadian National Railway and other companies. The three companies are the Toronto Terminals Railway Company, the Northern Alberta Railway Company, the Chicago and Western Indiana Railroad Company.
The method used in supplying new equipment or in making capital expenditures on the properties of these companies is that securities are issued of which the Canadian National Railways purchases part. Their contribution, in other words, to the capital expenditures of these three railway systems for 1938 will be $700,000.

Whether this may not go too far I am in some doubt. It looks to me as though possibly it goes further than it should-this idea of condonation, and making them liable for acts that are done if the knowledge is brought home to them. That, it seems to me, is extremely difficult. subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE CERTAIN EXEMPTIONS AND ADDITIONAL REGULATIONS
speechtext:
There is a matter to which I should like to direct the attention of the committee at this time-I know that for the last two years the minister has been made acquainted with it-and it has to do with the excise tax known as the sugar tax. In Canada there is a primary industry, forming part of the great industry of agriculture, known as the fruit and vegetable industry. Of the products of this industry it is necessary to preserve a large quantity in cans in order that provision may be made for their consumption at other seasons of the year. The complaint is that this industry is subject to the sugar tax while imported fruits and vegetables in the same form are not so handicapped. The manufacturer of canned fruits and vegetables in Canada, also of jams, jellies and marmalades, pays a tax of one cent per pound on the sugar used as an ingredient in the finished product. The complete exemption from this tax accorded to imported canned fruits and vegetables and the freedom from the tax of substitute domestic products such as are listed here-honey, maple syrup, peanut butter, and so on, which are competitive with jams-places this industry, we believe, in an entirely different position from that of certain other industries in justifying the granting of relief from the tax. The tax collected from this industry in 1936 was $608,996, representing between 20 and 25 per cent of the value of the sugar used.
This tax is not applied by the government on the sugar content of imported processed fruits and vegetables, which means that the manufacturer abroad is placed at an advantage over the Canadian producer of identical lines to the extent of this sugar tax. The special war revenue excise tax, subsection 6 of section 80, provides that the sugar excise tax shall be imposed on the sugar content of imported goods, but as stated, this provision has not been invoked in respect to processed fruits and vegetables. It is the desire of the Canadian industry that they be placed on a parity in respect to exemption from the sugar excise tax with producers of like goods shipping their products into this country.
The production in Canada of processed fruits, with a sugar cost varying from 7i to 25 per cent of the material and labour cost in the case of fruits preserved in syrup, and to over 50 per cent of the material cost in the case of jam in the year 1936-the latest period for which figures are available-was $10,132,383.
51952-273J
Special War Revenue Act
Exports were $1,495,969, leaving $8,636,414 as the domestic consumption. All of the sales in Canada carried the excise tax.
During 1936 the importations of canned fruits, and so on, were $1,771,255. None of the foregoing imports paid the excise tax, and analysis of those imports shows that in 1936 they comprised 26,205,704 pounds of canned pineapple, chiefly from Singapore, and 5,119,740 pounds of peaches, pears, apricots, principally from Australia in 1936, and about 1,000,000 pounds of miscellaneous processed fruits from other sources.
While the Singapore pineapple is not directly competitive with an identical Canadian product, there can be no doubt that its cheapness-about 3 cents per pound as compared with 8 cents per pound for honey and 10 cents per pound for jam-owing to the conditions under which it is manufactured, and which cheapness is accentuated by freedom from excise tax on its sugar content, has greatly facilitated its sale in Canada, and that this has tended to displace to a considerable degree Canadian canned fruit. It might be mentioned incidentally that this imported canned pineapple enters free of duty.
In the case of jam, jellies and marmalade, in which by far the largest proportion of sugar is used in any of the branches of the industry, while they are not subject to the same extent as canned fruits to the competition of imports, they are in direct competition with other domestic products which are not subject to the excise tax and which have the still greater advantage of exemption from sales tax. Some of these commodities are peanut butter, tabfe syrup, and honey.
I have here a table giving the production of peanut butter and honey for the five year period 1932-36, but it is not necessary for me
to put it on Hansard. I may point out, however, that honey has a sugar content of approximately 75 per cent. As an illustration, the sugar tax represents, as an item of cost in the production of jam, from 7i per cent to 12J per cent, but when it is borne in mind that this item of cost also carries the sales tax, the above percentages would be increased. The effect of these taxes including the sales tax brings it up to 27 per cent of the total cost on jam, which is the poor man's product. The complaint is that the tax is applied to the goods sold on the domestic market and not applied to those imported.

speechtext: That is the second consideration. The difficulty about exempting sugar used by manufacturers of canned goods is that it would undoubtedly lead to other exemptions. It would be impossible-or it has always been so felt-to remove the one cent sugar tax from manufacturers without also removing it for housewives and people generally who use sugar for canning and preserving. I am afraid there would immediately be a great outcry about discrimination if we lifted the tax from the manufacturer and not from the ordinary user, the housewife who is using sugar for canning and preserving. It is true that the imported product has an advantage, provided there is not a corresponding sugar tax in the country from which the product comes. It must not be assumed that the competitors of our canners in other countries are themselves free of tax in their own countries. In fact they are not; there is high taxation in nearly every country in the world to-day. At the worst I would point out that this discrimination, if such it is, merely cuts down somewhat the protection which the fruit canner in Canada enjoys. He does enjoy protection. There are duties I think on practically all canned goods coming into the country. If he were relieved of the sugar tax he would have a little more protection, that is all.

It is not altogether a question of protection; it is a question of opportunity to sell our own products on the home market in competition with the imported article. It has been pointed out. in a brief which I believe has been presented to the minister, that the difficulty might be overcome by way of drawback. I realize that it would be impossible to exempt this particular industry from the one cent tax. but it could be done by drawback, thus giving the Canadian industry an opportunity to compete with the imported product. I know the difficulty this industry has run up against in connection with exports to Great Britain. If the exported fruit is processed with sugar, a sugar tax must be paid when it enters Great Britain, but if it is shipped in sulphur dioxide form there is

We do not change the law at all so far as the use of the word "may" or "shall" is concerned; we say "fourteen or more days." It is only those words that are being changed.

I should like to revert to page 3 and to inquire of the minister whether any consideration was given in committee to section 124, which does not appear in the draft proposals. If not I should like to bring to the attention of the committee the kind of advertising that is done on many of our news-stands in the way of display of cheap magazines, selling for five, ten and fifteen cents, depicting shooting scenes. Section 124 has to do with gun pointing, I believe. I hold in my hand covers taken from forty or fifty magazines of this type, printed in Canada, showing scenes in colours of one person pointing a gun at another or shooting another. Many people with whom I have discussed the matter are very strongly of the opinion that this seriously tends to educate growing boys to think that there is nothing
Criminal Code

wrong about pointing a gun at a person, and as a result we see boys playing at bandit and hold-ups; we see them behind trees pointing toy guns and air guns at one another and even at passers-by.
I would not propose interfering with the contents of these magazines, but I think it is entirely wrong and detrimental to the morals of the boys that they should be permitted as they do to observe and study on magazine counters scenes such as these that are constantly placed before them. These covers could very well carry other pictures in colours to make the magazines attractive, such as pictures of men finely developed physically, beautiful women, floral or pastoral scenes, or scenes showing the resources of our country or our industries. But we should not be constantly placing before our boys scenes tending to educate them to think that there is nothing wrong in one person pointing a gun at another.
Accordingly I should like the minister to accept an amendment to this section to meet this situation. It would be in this form:
Everyone is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a penalty not exceeding one hundred dollars or to imprisonment for auy term not exceeding thirty days, with or without hard labour, who prints, makes or publishes any book or magazine on the cover of which appears any picture or drawing depicting the pointing by one person of an offensive weapon at another person or persons or the shooting by one person of another person or persons with such weapon, if such picture or drawing is intended to or does illustrate or represent a hold-up, robbery, murder or other criminal act or intention.
I have omitted in this proposed amendment one provision that I had earlier under consideration, namely to make it an offence to sell or expose to public view for sale or to distribute or circulate such books or magazines. But it was pointed out that such a provision would make the legislation very difficult of enforcement; consequently I have eliminated it.
Mr. LAPOINTE (Quebec East); I appreciate the motive and purpose of my hon. friend's amendment, but I have been considering it, and I cannot feel that I could accept it. If the picture of a man pointing a gun was inside the cover it would be permitted, and I find it difficult to see that it should be made a crime to put such a picture on the outside of the cover when it is not illegal to put it inside. And then, since it can be put inside, it would not take the boys or other persons who like that sort of thing very long to learn that they could find these pictures by simply opening the book. The law now makes it a crime to point any firearm or air-gun at any person; that is punished 
by a severe penalty, but I really cannot see my way clear to accept an amendment making it a crime merely to put such a picture on the cover of a book.

There are one or two matters that arose during the debate last evening to which I should like to refer. The important part of this section is not the mere nationalization of the bank but the policy that will be carried out when the bank is brought under the complete control of the

Bank of Canada
government. I should like to know from the minister in charge just what changes in policy, if any, are contemplated. In what way will the establishment of complete ownership change the policy of controlling the issue of currency and credit so that the domestic and general needs of the country may be more efficiently served? If there is to be no change in policy, then the real purpose of ownership will not be achieved. After all, this is a fairly expensive experiment that we are carrying on, and I should like to hear from the minister on that point.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of National Revenue, for Mr. Dunning):
subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC
speechtext:
The purposes
for which the bank is set up are set out in the preamble to the act. The policy of the bank will be to carry out the objects set out in the preamble. I do not know that it is possible to be any more definite than that. The bank is now under the control of the government and the action of its board of directors will, of course, reflect the policy of the government from time to time. The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Mc-Geer) must realize that it is not usual to announce a policy for any substantial period in advance. In fact, quite often in response to questions asked in this house it has been stated that the policy of the government will be made known as circumstances develop. I believe that answer is appropriate here, subject, of course, to the overruling consideration that the purposes of the bank, as set out in the preamble, must at all times be kept in mind.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC
speechtext:
Our present law permits our banks to create bank deposits for the purpose of increasing currency and credit in circulation on a five per cent reserve basis. Last evening the minister seemed to condone the attitude of the bank that in banking practice that should be raised to ten per cent. If the banks can raise the reserve limit from five to ten per cent, there will be nothing to prevent their raising it to fifty per cent, if they so desire. There is a distinction between English and Canadian banks which was not sufficiently taken into account in the discussion last evening. Apparently we have all the machinery necessary for creating an abundance of credit currency which would be available to the national government for public development, but unfortunately while we have gone unorthodox in the creation of credit, we remain orthodox in the use of credit. In a word, we have created a twentieth century monetary system, but as far as policy is concerned we still remain on a nineteenth century theory basis.
There was another distinction that apparently was not clear to the minister, judging from his remarks last evening. Of the total cash available in Canada to meet public need, till money, out of pocket transactions, international exchange obligations and interbank balances, there is owned outright by the banks $247,000,000 of Bank of Canada bills of issue. We have $102,000,000 of Bank of Canada bills of issue and circulating to the banks in the hands of the public. In addition to that, according to the Bank of Canada report we have $100,000,000 of banking currency which functions for all the purposes of till money and for out of pocket transactions, making a total of $449,000,000. Now to service our bank deposits, $2,800,000,000, even on the 10 per cent reserve basis that the banks of England require, we would still have a surplus of cash circulating in Canada of $161,000,000, or sufficient for an increase of banking deposits in Canada, even on the 10 per cent reserve basis, of $1,600,000,000.
What I am pointing out now is this, that although we have, even on the bank's basis, $1,600,000,000 of unused bank deposits available, supposedly under the control of the country and the government, and we are now going to increase that control by paying a substantial profit to get those shares which were handed out as a concession in 1934 back into public ownership, the question still remains how are we going to get the currency and credit which is available into circulation for the benefit of the people of Canada? And that was the thing that this bank was created to establish.
I should like to make one reference to a statement that was made by the leader of the opposition. He saw fit to point out that bank deposits had to be represented by something, and that they could not increase beyond bank holdings of securities. But since 1934. when this concession was handed over to the private banks, bank deposits have increased by $479,000,000, while the holding of government interest-bearing bonds by the chartered banks has increased by $471,000,000. The point I should like to draw to the attention of the minister and of the government is that in so far as the use of that increase of credit is concerned during the period of four years that the Bank of Canada has been in operation, that increase of credit has apparently been available only for the purchase of government bonds by the chartered banks.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC
speechtext: Was it not available for all purposes, but that was one purpose which was possible under existing economic conditions?

The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George states that it was avail-
Bank oj Canada

able for all purposes, and that is very true. But the reason why government control comes into being is that we believed that the banks were exercising a discretion as to whom they would advance money, and control was necessary to make the circulation effective to serve the needs of the country and the needs of progress.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC
speechtext: I do not care to interrupt, but would my hon. friend allow a question?

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC
speechtext: Is it not absolutely necessary that directors of the banks should have a discretion as to the persons or companies to whom they grant loans, in view of the fact that it is the directors alone who are responsible to the shareholders for the security of those loans? Can you possibly avoid conceding discretion, unless the government of Canada is going to guarantee repayment to the banks of all loans made, that is, in case you are going to restrict the discretion of the directors in making such loans?

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC
speechtext: I quite concede that, and that is one reason why I believe that merchant banking should be left exclusively to the merchant bankers, subject only to the control of the Bank of Canada, which would avoid those disastrous inflations which come with commodity and security booms. But that is a very different thing from the thing I am talking about. What I am dealing with is the question of how government in Canada can have freer access, at less cost, to the national currency and credit of the country, which the banks to-day are using to purchase bonds by the manipulation or by the actual use of a bookkeeping system. There is a very great difference between private finance and public finance, and the sooner we come to recognize that one of the great duties of the Bank of Canada is to establish a control of public finance that will completely segregate public finance from private finance, and that the two shall be established as entirely different services in the state, the better.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC
speechtext: I have listened frequently to the hon. member. Can he suggest how the aim which he has expressed can be accomplished more readily than under the present proposed system under which the government shall have complete control over the Bank of Canada and all its transactions?

I am going to suggest that now. What I am going to commend to the government-and I do not expect anything to be done this session-is that in addition to having the machinery which the Bank of Canada now has, an investigation be launched

to ascertain whether or not it would be advisable for the Bank of Canada to become the actual bank of the Dominion of Canada, serving it with a deposit and cheque system in exactly the same way that the chartered banks are serving it to-day; and whether, in turn, as is the case in Australia, there should be a bank established in each of the provinces as a branch of the Bank of Canada which would serve provincial and municipal governments in the same way.

A public body such as a workmen's compensation board, a body administering an unemployment insurance fund, or a host of other activities which involve the carrying of large deposits and large reserve funds, would carry them in the public banking institution.
The other point to which I wished to refer was this, The statement was made last

Bank of Canada
night that a ten per cent reserve of cash was necessary to prevent the banks from going into bankruptcy from day to day. Nothing could be more out of line with the history of banking in Canada than any such statement as that.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman will allow me, that statement was not made. The statement which was made was that, the bank directors being responsible for loans and for making only such loans as were likely to be repaid because of the financial stability or security of the persons to whom they were made, a provision of even ten per cent was not sufficient tor all times and all circumstances. No bank can agree that the mere holding of ten per cent security, as the hon. gentleman states, will be sufficient to protect the bank in times of grave economic and financial stress and strain. The directors must be sure that they have the funds wherewith to meet all demands when made, and for that purpose at certain times it may be necessary to keep, instead of five or ten per cent, twenty-five or thirty or even forty per cent available. It was found in time of crisis in the United States that even forty per cent was not always sufficient to protect the shareholders and depositors of banks.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC
speechtext:
Quite true. But the point I was dealing with was the point that came up last night, and it is to be found at page 4298 of Hansard, where the Minister of National Revenue said:
In other words, the banks are maintaining only the reserve ratio that is necessary in the light of experience, namely, approximately ten per cent.

Sufficient to keep them from day to day from going into bankruptcy?

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC

That is the point I was dealing with. If the hon. gentleman will remember, when he sat in this house there was a double shuffle of 835,000,000 that went out to the banks in and around 1933. That went out for a definite purpose, to meet the stress and strain which the depression had put upon the banks of Canada, and to put them in a position to meet their obligations among each other as much as anything else. There is the emergency reserve upon which the banks rely in times of emergency. It is a call upon the government to use the nation's money to protect institutions which have got into trouble because they have traded short in money and long in credit. Because that type of thing is done in the name of sound money, it goes
on as one of the most iniquitous things that any government has ever condoned. Now we go ahead and say that we are going to reduce the right of the banks of Canada to print money freely. In 1934 this house solemnly amended the Bank Act, to reduce what? The right of the banks of Canada to use a printing press to create money, so that it would come down ten per cent per annum until it was reduced to a twenty-five per cent quota of their paid-up capital.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC
speechtext: Does the hon. member object to that provision?

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC
speechtext: If the hon. member had been present and had understood the circumstances under which that was done, he would know that it was to meet a special emergency arising out of the bankruptcy of some three or four thousand banks in the United States.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC

To use the expression "racket," and other terms which the hon. gentleman has used, merely implies that he is entirely ignorant of or has not understood the special emergency which was met on that occasion. We protected the commerce and industry of Canada to a large extent, and with better results than commerce and industry were protected in the United States or in Australia or in any other dominion of the commonwealth.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC

speechtext: That is what it is created for.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC
speechtext: Yes, but that is not what happened at all. What has happened is this. The Bank of Canada has issued money to the banks for certain securities, but in the meantime it has purchased and acquired millions of dollars' worth of public securities for which it has put money out for nothing. As the Minister of Finance pointed out, no matter from whom the bank buys securities, when it issues legal tender cash that cash is bound to come to the banks. When the Bank of Canada maintains a policy of issuing legal tender cash in exchange for securities, the result is that the banks are supplied with money at less cost than they formerly were put to when they were called upon to print money.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC
speechtext: It is put in the banks by the depositors.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC
speechtext: What I am pointing out is that in the Bank of Canada report in May, for instance, we find the cash issues given and there is no liability at all against them. subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC

I will not argue the question further, but I wish to quote from an address delivered last night in Halifax, which was broadcast all over Canada and which I do not think either this government or any one else in this house should ignore. I quote:
The Liberal party cannot lead the people.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC

saying, but what Mr. Herridge stated in Halifax last night. He said:
The Liberal party cannot lead the people. For reaction leads it.
This party was born in the economy of scarcity. There it still abides. The present fact of potential plenty has no place in its philosophy. Though in the beginning, mark you, the Liberal party nailed to its masthead, the doctrine of political and economic freedom. And scarcity, of course, is the denial of all freedom.

Reaction dominates the Liberal party. The Liberal hierarchy, the party's high command, its unawakened followers, are for the old order and against the new.
The Liberal machine is the hired man of the money power. For a time, all that the money power asked of Liberalism was to be left alone. The Liberal party left it alone. But to-day, in government, to do nothing is to do wrong. The fixation of Liberalism has been a firm base for reaction's operations against the people.
The money power is against free trade. The Liberal party is against freedom of trade: except in speeches.
Before the last election, the Liberal leader promised to do battle with the money power. There has been no battle.
The startling thing about this speech is that it is addressed to a Conservative convention in Halifax pleading that the Conservatives line up against the money power and throw the leader of the Liberal government out of office because he has not done battle with that power.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC
speechtext: As promised.

speechtext:
Members on the other
side have said that I have strange ideas and have advanced strange doctrines, but I never dreamed that as a Liberal I should ever live to read this great effusion as the expression of Conservatism on the Atlantic shores of Canada. But time goes on. The Conservative party has had its place in the Dominion of Canada and goes down with other institutions that have fallen into the limbo of the things that merely decorate the memories of the past and stand obsolete in the way of progress. But let me say that as the Conservative party goes out there is a danger of the Liberal party becoming and remaining the Conservative party of the past.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC
speechtext: Becoming! It is.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC
speechtext:
We have a hope, a great hope, that this reactionary spirit of which even the Conservatives now complain, and which bristles in the banking policy of 1934 will go, not only on this side of the house but on that. This problem of establishing a new order which can finance progress is above party politics. If partyism fails to meet the challenge, which I believe this party is honestly making the effort to meet to-day, as badly as the party opposite failed during the years following the change of monetary policy in 1934, then a new national organization will take hold of the issue. The thing that won the election in Saskatchewan more than anything else was the promise of the Prime Minister to nationalize the Bank of Canada, meaning that he was going to give
[Mr. McGeer.J
this dominion a national monetary policy. We believe and hope that during the coming winter, before the next session of parliament, this monetary problem will be grappled with in Canada as it has been in other nations, and that along with a publicly owned institution to make our national monetary policy a public utility service we shall have a developed policy under which the administration will make that public utility service real and effective.

speechtext:
This discussion arose from the question asked of the acting minister concerning the control of the bank, and as to whether this section actually gave the government control of the Bank of Canada. We listened to the discussion with interest, and perhaps some valuable points were made. In the speeches made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) on this measure, particularly at the resolution stage, he declared, more than once, that the purpose of this bill was not to control the policy of the Bank of Canada. I have analysed those speeches carefully, and the minister clearly pointed out that the reason for the bill was to silence political controversy over the constitution of the Bank of Canada. I find that the minister used the terms "political controversy" and "political discussion" fifteen times in the two speeches that he made. In the course of the minister's speech the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) asked a question as to the political controversy that has taken place in the past few years being the reason for bringing down the bill. I quote from page 4055 of Hansard1 for June 20 last:
Mr. Woodsworth:	I have been listening to
what the minister has said, and I am in hearty sympathy with the purpose of the resolution, but I find it difficult to understand what has occurred in the last twelve months that has led this government to make this almost complete change in a policy which was adopted no doubt after careful deliberation. Can the minister give us further information on that point?
Mr. Dunning: I do not think I can go further than I have gone. It was quite evident to the government during the last two years that the constitution of the bank was becoming and would likely continue to be a matter of political controversy.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Burra-rd (Mr. McGeer) made a remark which was received with some enthusiasm, that the election in Saskatchewan was won largely because the Prime Minister had promised completely to nationalize the Bank of Canada. That may be so. I am not so much concerned about that, but I am concerned about the fact that the bill does seem to be a political move. Personally I feel confident

Bank of Canada
that this bill does not and is not necessarily designed to give to the government control of policy. If we could be assured that the policy of the bank was going to be changed so that the issue of currency and credit could be made in the interests of domestic commercial and industrial need, we would have more reason for voting for the bill. We are in favour in the bill, because we believe it is a step in the right direction, but if that step is only to put the entire directorate under the government we doubt very much whether it is such a very important step in the right direction.
As to the bill being a political bill, I am not saying this with any malice towards the government, because as the last speaker (Mr. McGeer) has said, the Liberals have a great hope. This group here would rejoice if the great hope that the hon. member had in mind were realized. The Liberal government will always find this group sympathetic to any forward move on behalf of democracy towards controlling the issuance of money in terms of public need. But to go back: it seems to me the bill is somewhat of a political bill. I have it in mind-the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) mentioned it the other day-that two years ago the Prime Minister said very distinctly, when the bill for the purchase of fifty-one per cent of the stock of the Bank of Canada was before the house, that that bill was designed to fulfil the promise that he had made prior to the election. Then -I am recalling this as I have a point to make-the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) in Edmonton was reported as saying that the complete control of currency and credit would be in the hands of the government by 1945. When that report came out in the press I asked the Prime Minister on the floor of the house whether we could expect any legislation to be brought down that would in any way readjust the banking system of this country. I thought that a legitimate question to ask after what the Minister of Agriculture had said in Edmonton. I think I can say in all kindness that the Prime Minister's answer to my question was vague. He told us that the legislative program would not be complete until the close of the session. I wonder whether the Prime Minister had in mind then that the government would be bringing down this bill.

If the central bank of a country is to serve the high purpose for which it is created, it must be manned by men who not only are expert in monetary, economic and financial matters, but also have a sufficient independence of judgment to be able at all times to talk on equal terms to the government of the day with respect to the matters which come under the jurisdiction of the bank in the ordinary course of business.
There may be some value in the government listening not only to those who may be appointed to the directorate but also to members of parliament who come here representing sections of this great democracy that are demanding results along the lines of economic reform. To be honest with the Minister of Finance in connection with the quotation I just read I should say that the minister did go on, at page 4059, to say:
The general broad policy of the bank of course must be in harmony with the desires of a majority of this parliament.
I am glad that statement was made, because I do feel that the policy of the Bank of Canada should be determined by the desires of the members of this house, who after all represent this great democracy.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC
speechtext: The remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer) a moment ago began with a question addressed to the Minister of National Revenue, who is in charge of this bill. The hon. member wanted to know what the government's policy was going to be, and the minister replied that it was not usual to declare government policy in advance. I believe, however, that we should have a definite statement as to what is meant by government policy. It will be remembered by all hon. members of this house and by the people of this country that the Liberal party intended to take hold of the Bank of Canada and issue currency and credit in terms of public need. We are not asking for a statement of policy, but it does seem to me that we have a right to ask, and that we should insist upon knowing, what is meant by public need. What is meant by issuing credit and currency in terms of public need? If a satisfactory explanation is given in that regard it is not necessary to know what the policy will be.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC

Bank of Canada

frequently interpreted it. It means exactly what it says, in terms of public need as distinct from private gain; it is not synonymous, and could not possibly be, with individual private need.

I want to know what is meant by public need, and I believe the people of the country are entitled to have a proper definition of that term.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman-

There is little difficulty in defining the general objectives of the central bank and of the government which controls it. These objectives are the maximum possible sustained level of productivity and the minimum possible level of unemployment.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC

Bank of Canada

speechtext: Will the Prime Minister say that the Bank of Canada is going to issue credit and currency in order to create employment? subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC

speechtext:

Undoubtedly that day is coming, but because up to the present the situation has not been made clear it may serve a good purpose to clarify it on this occasion.
To-day there is no combined or effective opposition to the Liberal party. There are in Canada various schools of progressive thought, but none sufficiently large of itself to offer effective opposition to the present government. But I feel sure that, with the alignment of all progressive thought in Canada in order to accomplish greater abundance in this life for the common people, there will develop a definite forward movement against the forces of reaction. I merely wish to point this out because of the remarks of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, and to assure him, even though we have not his experience and have not arrived at his age in life, it is a principle of democracy that the will of democracy must eventually prevail. subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC
speechtext:
I quite understand that the minister, who is very ably taking the place of the Minister of Finance, would hardly be prepared to make any alteration in the section, but I must point out that to leave this section as it now stands will, I think, be found extremely embarrassing to the government. I believe they will have to amend it next session. The minister will recall that in the section passed in 1936 we provided for the retirement of directors in 1940, 1941, and as late as 1942. It is obvious that as the section now before the committee reads these members of the present board will retire only on the last day of February in their respective years. I should say that the government would find it highly desirable to provide for their retirement at once, or at least at the end of February of next year, and then re-appoint them, if desired, because provision is made here for re-appointment; otherwise I think the government is going to be embarrassed. I say that frankly. We have continued these directors in office until the February preceding the expiration of their term of office. It Will be recalled that in the 1936 section-without going into it at length- we provided for two to retire at the annual
Bank of Canada

meeting in 1940, two in 1941, two in 1942 and so on. Now we repeal the section, and there is no longer any authority for their appointment; that has vanished. There are no annual meetings in the sense heretofore provided; therefore there can be no appointments at the annual meetings. But in the section now under consideration we also say that:
The minister with the approval of the governor in council shall as of the first day of March in each year appoint for terms of three years each a sufficient number of directors to provide that there shall be eleven directors: provided, however, that every director holding office at the date of the coming into force of this subsection shall continue as a director up to and including the last day of February in the year of the expiration of the term of office for which he was elected or appointed.
This, of course, means that whatever policy the government may desire to embark upon, there is no power to remove the directors unless you come back to parliament. The policy of the government is reflected by the board, and the government should be in a position to put in its board of directors at least by next February. This can be brought about in the manner I have indicated. I am not going to do more than direct attention to the matter, because I realize the position of the minister.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC
speechtext:
There is a majority of
government appointed directors on the board at the present time, and as far as I know there has been no criticism of the shareholder appointed directors, who are in the minority. Both are satisfactory.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC
speechtext: But those appointed by the government are appointed with definite limitations, and they will continue in office for a considerable length of time. Whether or not they would reflect the policy of the government with a government owned institution as distinguished' from a government controlled institution is a matter which obviously the government is not going to discuss. I am content as long as I have directed attention to the fact that I think the government will want to come back later and change the section.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC

I am worrying about the shares, and I am thinking of the treasury. This little transaction is costing the treasury of this country $920,000, and from a logical, sound, common sense basis I cannot see why we should issue $50 shares in 1934 and then buy them back at $5920 in 1938. They were a gilt-edged security paying 4i per cent all the way

Bank of Canada
through, and they went up in price only because it was practically certain that the interest would be paid during the term of the shares. speechtext: No.

Yes. In my opinion that
price represents the speculative value placed upon them. If we had securities yielding five per cent, these shares would not have gone up so much; on the other hand, if government securities yielded only 2i per cent, these shares would have gone much higher. Bank of Canada

corporate existence. It is not a department of government; it is a corporation, a body politic. As I said before, I do not see anything in the circumstances to effect the release of the government's liability.

subtopic: ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT OP SHARES NOW IN HANDS OF THE PUBLIC
speechtext: Some of our Canadian banks are carrying on operations outside Canada. If they were to become insolvent because of acts committed outside Canada, it would affect Canadians. Surely I could not put it any more clearly than I have in the proposition I put before the committee. We pay $4,500,000 because they are three per cent securities. The Dominion of Canada is now responsible. There is no getting away from that; that is the whole argument upon which this bill proceeds. speechtext:
Right Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to incorporate a commission with power under the Minister of Justice to administer, control and manage the penitentiaries; to provide for salaries of the commissioners and assistant commissioners and to amend and consolidate the Penitentiaries Act and amending acts and repeal the same.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: INCORPORATION OF COMMISSION FOR ADMINISTRATION, CONTROL AND MANAGEMENT-AMENDMENT OF EXISTING ACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will expedite business by agreeing to your honour leaving the chair without prejudice to the position which I propose to take with respect to this resolution. Perhaps it can be more readily

discussed in committee. I must say, however, that I have a very strong opinion against our proceeding with this matter at this time for
reasons that I shall presently give.
Motion agreed to, and the house went into committee, Mr. Johnston (Lake Centre) in the chair.

subtopic: INCORPORATION OF COMMISSION FOR ADMINISTRATION, CONTROL AND MANAGEMENT-AMENDMENT OF EXISTING ACTS
speechtext:
I am hopeful that the Minister of Justice will not ask us to deal with this matter at this late date in the
session.
Here is a measure of first-rate importance. I use the word "first-rate" in the sense in which it was employed by an old parliamentary draftsman, as denoting a measure which profoundly affects the whole country and no one particular section of it.
A royal commission has made a report. That report was not laid on the table of this house until the fourteenth day of June. The evidence upon which the report was made should also be laid on the table, and I suppose that in due course it will be, but it is not yet available.
The report is a highly contentious document. I am receiving letters from many people complaining of the absolute unfairness, and more, the absolute untruthfulness of statements made in that report. In a public newspaper, for instance, Messrs. Morris of Kingston have published a letter in connection with the handling of coal. The coal was unloaded at a dock. They estimated they had unloaded 250 tons, but it was subject to being measured and weighed. It was weighed and it was found that there were only 217 tons. They sent up the balance of the coal, got receipts for it, and were paid for it; yet they were pilloried in that report. I might cite page after page.
I wonder whether the committee is aware of the fact that this is the first time in our history that as a parliament we are invited to remove a man from office upon the report of a commission which gave him practically no opportunity to be heard. I wonder whether hon. members realize just how the evidence was taken, whose evidence it was, and the conditions under which it was given.
I wish to tell the committee something as to the appointment of General Ormond. He was not appointed by the previous government. The civil service commission was asked to appoint someone to be superintendent of penitentiaries. Advertisements were published throughout this country. Among those who applied for the position was General Ormond, who at that time was district officer commanding at Calgary. He is a pronounced Liberal, as are the members of his family.

Penitentiaries Commission Act
When the applications were completed, the then Minister of Justice-I recall the fact vividly-was spoken to by the civil service commission, and informed that they had a number of applications. Thereupon the following were appointed to consider them: the late General MacBrien; Mr. 0. M. Biggar, K.C.; Mr. Edwards, K.C., Deputy Minister of Justice; representing the Department of Justice; Colonel Kemmis, representing the civil service commission; Mr. Dufresne, director of public safety, Montreal; and Doctor Porteous, head of the medical side of the institution for mental diseases, Verdun. Those gentlemen considered all the applications received by the commission, and upon the strength of the recommendation made by them the commission appointed General Ormond to that office. That is the story of his appointment.
He has been pilloried in the report. I have great confidence in the fairness of mind of the minister in a matter of this kind. I commenced what I have said by remarking that this is non-political. Having established that it is non-political, I then have great confidence in the fair-mindedness of the Minister of Justice. Is it quite right that one who had a distinguished record in the great war, who occupied a position of high importance in the permanent militia of this country and was well spoken of, who in the ordinary course would have gone from the Calgary command to one more important, should now be confronted with such action as is proposed upon the report of a commission which investigated and took evidence in many quarters from convicts and, after all this was done, brought him up, put him under oath and grilled him by examination and cross-examination? Did you ever hear of the governor of an English prison being treated in that way? Is that, Mr. Chairman, your conception of British fair play and justice?
Strange as it may sound, I barely know the gentleman. If I have seen him ten times, that would be the maximum. He came to Calgary when I was away as leader of the opposition; but I am familiar with the circumstances of his appointment, and I verified my recollection as to the board which recommended his appointment to the civil service commission. Should we not do something a little more decent than is now contemplated to a man of this type? Should we, in the closing days of the session, without the evidence having been laid on the table or our having an opportunity to study it, with the house meeting three times a day, with committees in session, with hon. members unable to examine this very important report, undertake to make ourselves parties to the 51952-275
condemnation of this man? Frankly, having endeavoured to think of the matter as fairly as one can think of anything, I cannot bring myself to believe that we are as unfair as that.
There is one other point. This is dealing with the administration of an extremely important branch of the social life of Canada. Penal institutions have existed for many centuries. The manner of their administration has many times been the subject of investigation and criticism. As a consequence, great improvements were wrought by Howard and those associated with him. Our penal institutions are being maintained for two purposes', one, the punishment of the offender; two, to endeavour so to improve his character that he might be a not unuseful member of society when he left prison. There has never been a time that I can remember in my reading when those who were the victims of their own wrong-doing and had been subjected to the results, by sentences of punishment and imprisonment, have not complained of those whom the law placed in authority to enforce the decrees of society. That is the reason why these people have complained of General Ormond. That is the explanation of this tittle-tattle. There is nothing new about it. It is as old as time itself, and I cannot think that we should set at naught the conditions under which this man came into our service without at least obeying the law itself.
I put this to the minister. Ormond is a civil servant, and he is subject to the provisions of the Civil Service Act. If he is incapable, he must have the allegations of his incapacity charged against him, and he must be given the fullest opportunity to make his defence. Did he have that opportunity? And since when, in this country, has it been possible for three men, without responsibility to this parliament, to arrogate to themselves the right to dismiss this man-for that is what it amounts to-without his having those safeguards with which the law surrounds him made effective in his behalf? I put that as number one. I find it very difficult to accommodate my mind to any other thought. How would we like to be placed in that position? Here is a man appointed under the circumstances that I have mentioned, who sought office in the public service, and who was filling a fine position. His credentials are passed upon by a dispassionate, impartial, nonpolitical tribunal. The civil service board makes the appointment, and then I contend he becomes subject to the Civil Service Act, and can be removed from office only in consequence of his having contravened the provisions of that statute. Has he done so?



Penitentiaries Commission Act
Who says so? And we, as a parliament, we the members of this house are the people that are concerned. We said to Ormond when he went into that service under the Civil Service Act, " There is what governs you, Mr. Ormond ; if you are guilty of political partisanship, you know what happens. If you contravene any of the sections of the act, out you go; but you do not go until you are heard."
I often recall in that regard what was done in the West Indies where a judge sitting on the bench made it impossible for his creditors to recover against him. He was finally dismissed from office, and properly so; but when the case went before the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, they said, "The conduct of this man is indefensible, but you cannot remove a man who has the queen's commission unless he has had an opportunity to make his defence, even though you know he cannot make a successful defence." That, in my judgment, is the strongest reason why we should not proceed this session.
I go a step further. It will be recalled that the proposed bill provides for the appointment of commissioners to control and manage our penitentiaries. We have never embarked upon such an experiment in Canada. Since pre-confederation days this matter was the responsibility of government, and government accepted the full responsibility. Three men are now to deal with the matter. The experience of history, whatever it may be worth-and I always think it is worth a great deal-is that when you divide responsibility of that ldnd, which is administrative, among three men on a commission, you lessen efficiency and bring about the very condition which you endeavour to .prevent and for which administrative control exists. I ask any member of this committee to think back, consider this matter and say whether he has not found that precisely what I say is true. It is one man's direction that always makes for efficient administration in an administrative body. You appoint three, and you have inevitably a condition that is repugnant to your very notion of effectiveness. Every one knows that. When you are dealing with the civil service commission, of course, you want diversity; when you are dealing with the board of railway commissioners, that is not wholly administrative; but here is an administrative arm of government under the Minister of Justice. The Minister of Justice is going to be the responsible minister who reports to this house, and under him, instead of there being as heretofore one man who looks after matters, controls and directs, there 
will be three. They meet together and discuss; two think one thing and one thinks another, and you have all the resultant inefficiency that comes from three administrative heads with respect to a matter for which the Minister of Justice is carrying the responsibility.
Then follows that other recommendation which is involved in this, the question of the parole system, which it is proposed shall be administered by these three commissioners. In the first place the Minister of Justice will agree with me that there is at the threshold of the discussion the question of the prerogative. The prerogative is that of the sovereign, and until recent years the instructions that issued to His Excellency the Governor General carried with them the right on his part to exercise the high prerogative of mercy. Originally he did it without reference to his advisers; he had himself to administer that prerogative. Now the instructions of the governor general provide that the prerogative of mercy is exercised on the advice of the government. The Minister of Justice reports to council, and council adopts his recommendation, or otherwise, as the case may be. That is to be swept out. The prerogative of mercy is no longer the prerogative right of the sovereign; it is to be handled by a parole board.
I am not for a moment saying that there may not be merit in that contention, but I am saying that I have not had any opportunity to study it. I have not had the opportunity, which it is so essential that one should have, of studying the matter in order to be able to discuss it intelligently. What is more, I want to see the evidence.

I think the one that
should be most carefully weighed is the one we are now considering. That disposes of the parole question; for the minister has said that it is not proposed in this measure to adopt the recommendation which gives to the commission the powers of a parole board. We can therefore leave that.
There are a number of other subsidiary questions; but I implore the minister, more

Penitentiaries Commission Act
than. 1 ever have with respect to any matter I can remember considering in this house, not to permit us to put ourselves on record, in the closing days of the session

we expect to close in the next three or four days at least-as changing the whole system of the administration of the penitentiaries of this country.
Dismissals are involved. It was a great mistake that one member of the commission should have accepted appointment; for he was the one who appeared as counsel when Inspector Dawson was charged before Judge Daly. He has now slated Dawson and held him up as the embodiment of, shall I say inefficiency. Now he signs that report.
I entreat the minister to think of a man who values highly his reputation, a man who has not communicated with me either directly or indirectly, a man whom I scarcely know, who is opposed to me politically, whose family all his life has been actively associated with the Liberal party, a man who faced death in many forms in the slime and dirt of France and Flanders, who came back and sought honourable employment under the crown, and who was given a position, and believed, as I did, that the Civil Service Act enacted by the parliament of Canada contained the terms and conditions of his employment. Now a body not responsible to us has treated him in a manner, I make bold to say, wholly unwarranted by any evidence that could be properly adduced before a judicial tribunal. I know, from the investigations and; inquiries which I set on foot and, from reading some of that evidence, that it would not stand for a moment before a judicial body. It is the evidence of men who have been placed away from society as menaces to society, men who, to use the language of my old preceptor in law, had to be removed from society because they were like mad dogs running wild. These men, not one or two but a long line of them, tell their stories about Ormond, who at last is brought in and made subject to crossexamination by these three commissioners. On the strength of that I am asked to give my assent to a bill which removes him from office and replaces him with a commission. Does any such commission exist in England, Australia, or New Zealand? It may in some American states, but never in British countries as far as I have been able to discover in the limited time I have had at my disposal. The time for consideration is not sufficient; therefore I speak entirely subject to correction.
I have been endeavouring to look into this whole question. I visited prisons in Australia; I visited Borstal institutes in New 51952-2751
Zealand, and I have made some study of prison conditions in Great Britain. I visited a penitentiary in Canada, which is more than some can say. I went through the institution at Kingston; I saw the cells. When I read of men daring to sign a report six years after the events in question, and expect me to accept it, placing odium and discredit and disgrace upon men who value their reputations as highly as they, and compare that report with that of men who based their findings upon their knowledge of conditions as they existed at the moment, not six years after, to me it almost seems that we are not in a British country at all. I read the other day a magazine article in connection with what had taken place in Russia and how men are induced to plead guilty there. The story was told at some length by one who had been a prosecutor in Russia. Then I thought of this report, of the long row of convicts marching in, giving evidence against Ormond-

I am sorry if the hon.
member's conscience bothers her. There they are, a long line of them coming into a room. How long had they been at Kingston? What took place there? Have hon. members heard? Has the minister heard? Has he investigated? Does he realize what took place? Who were there? There is the long line; they march in just as they did in Russia; they tell their story and march out. Where was Ormond? He was doing his job here in his office. And that is Canada! That is British justice! That is the sort of thing I am asked in the closing days of a session to agree to.
I entreat the minister to let this matter stand until another session, in order that we may make ourselves familiar with this report, understand it in detail. I was going to ask him if he would lay on the table the evidence upon which this commission acted-I know he will-to enable us to see to what extent the findings are warranted. Some of them the minister says he does not propose to act upon. Of course he does not; why should he? Would any reputable minister act upon some of them? All I can do is entreat that in the exercise of his great power at this moment he will see to it that an opportunity is given to every hon. member of the House of Commons and the Senate of Canada to consider not only the report in detail but the implications of it, the evidence upon which it is founded, and to determine for himself and herself whether or not there is
Penitentiaries Commission Act

justification for such a radical change in the whole administration of our penal institutions as this bill involves.
I said I visited the penitentiary at Kingston. I have seen others, but I visited the Kingston penitentiary without notice. I saw the kind of food they were serving. I went right in; the warden was not even there; I went through the institution, saw the cells, saw these so-called places of punishment, saw the paddles that they used in connection with punishment, and I say that without question, the- penitentiaries of this country, which were administered for nearly nine years, from 1921 to 1930, by the present Minister of Justice- I forget whether he was Minister of Justice all that time-

Finally I say this. How many members of this committee, on both sides of the house, have had an opportunity to study the report of the commission? I know some who have read until late at night; but they have had committees in the morning, the house in the afternoon and again until eleven o'clock in the evening, correspondence on Saturdays and so on. How many have read that report? How many have given it that consideration upon which they could find a fellow citizen guilty; for that is what it amounts to? We are asked to record a verdict of guilty against these men, and not only to record it but to make it effective. That is why I venture to ask the right hon. Minister of Justice, in the exercise of his great power and authority in the position which he occupies, to remember that within the next few months a commission could not effect any great changes; that the penal system of this country, which has been administered as well as that of any other country in the world during the last several years, is not going to suffer by being administered in the same way for the next few months, and that between now and the time parliament meets again the fullest opportunity will be afforded to enable us to consider not only the radical changes involved but everything concerning the effective, efficient and useful administration-and I use the word "useful" as affecting the nation as a whole-of the penal system of Canada.

I have often said to many people that I think the right hon. leader of the opposition is the best informed man in the House of Commons on the greatest variety of subjects-I even went so far as to say on all subjects-but now I am afraid I must make one exception, and that is in regard to the penitentiaries of Canada. I am sure anyone who has made anything like a detailed study of the penitentiaries in different countries would not say that Canada has had as fine an administrative system as any other country in the world. That is going a very long way from the truth.
I do not want to make a lengthy speech at this time, but I do want to say that the one commissioner to whom the right hon. gentleman referred as having appeared before the Daly inquiry presumably would be Mr. McRuer, who was counsel at that inquiry. May I say that Mr. McRuer's services at that time were made available as a result of his interest in the subject. He never received a cent from anyone for what he did then. The penitentiary files that Mr. McRuer and I went over together at that time-and the right hon. leader of the opposition might be interested to know that they contain a detailed account about myself; for with his pointing to the convicts in this direction-

If they have not my finger-prints and photograph, at least they have a detailed story about me in the penitentiary files of this country, together with all the editorials against me but none in favour of me. It was the things which Mr. McRuer and I saw in those files, and the things we heard before that Daly commission, that convinced him that there was something very wrong with our whole system; that it was filled with intrigue and vindictiveness, and that something ought to be done about it. Since he is not here to speak for himself, as he could so well, I want to make this statement. Mr. McRuer, as the right hon. leader of the opposition knows, is a great counsel. He need not have accepted appointment as a member of the commission to which he was later appointed, and certainly he did not undertake that work with any thought of gain for himself. He took it because he was convinced, through the Daly inquiry, of the need for a thorough and wholesale house-cleaning.

I do not want to talk about General Ormond; but anyone who read the rules and regulations, and the interpretations of those rules and regulations, issued by General Ormond himself, would know, without having been in a penitentiary at all, if he was a sensible human being-as I am sure all members of parliament are-before this commission was ever appointed that this man was not a person who should be in charge of the penitentiaries of Canada. Many a time he boasted to minor officials that there were four or five interpretations of one rule or regulation. That alone would condemn him in the mind of any right thinking person. The prisoner was always wrong; he could not possibly be right, because if he appeared likely to succeed under one interpretation they could give another interpretation of the same rule, under which the prisoner would be condemned.
It is true that the commission has taken two years to do its work, which is a long time. It was slow in getting started. Calamity befell one or two people appointed to it at first. It did -take a long time to get started, and it did take a long time to make this study, but I do not think anyone who has read even a part of the report could fail to agree that it made a careful study. The commission did investigate the Borstal system in England. General Ormond came back and told us he had inaugurated a Borstal system in Canada. Anyone even moderately well informed on penitentiaries knew then that he had not done any such thing. It is a pity that any one person has to be condemned when he is not here to defend himself, but I am not particularly concerned about any one person in this affair. What is going to happen if we do as the right hon. leader of the opposition wishes, and take no action? We shall not only leave in office a superintendent who has been condemned, but also leave senior officers here and there who have been condemned as well. We shall then have a penal system under which the prisoners will have no confidence in -their superiors or in the system itself. If we go home without doing anything, I think I know enough about penitentiaries to say that we may have a great deal of disquiet and a repetition of the riots and near riots which have occurred so often during the regime of General Ormond. We cannot leave the report as it is. Something must be done in one way or another.
