speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the subject of this bill, and its bedfellow, Bill No. 7, was remitted to the committee on banking and commerce for study. This matter was studied during this session by that committee, as it was studied last session. After hearing witnesses and giving consideration to the reference to it, the committee presented a report to the house. That report was far from being unanimous; indeed there was sharp controversy in the committee with regard to the principles involved in the report. While the votes will show that the report of the committee was carried with only a small quorum present, there are some interesting facts to be disclosed from a study of the votes taken in the committee. I think it will be found that if all those who were opposed to the principles of the report had been in committee at the same time, the- vote might have been reversed. There was a sharp division of opinion with regard to the whole subject.
The report of the committee on banking and commerce respecting small loan companies carried with it a draft bill which is described as "An Act respecting Interest on Small Loans." This bill consists of a preamble, a number of definitions and two parts. Part II is said to apply to small loan companies incorporated by special acts of the parliament of Canada. In other words, this part is applicable only to those incorporations that are dominion in character. Part I is applicable to all money-lenders, as defined in the bill. 'Some important provisions are contained in section 2, which has to do with definitions, and also in section 3. I should like to direct attention to the definition of "cost," which is as follows:
(a) "Cost" of a loan means the whole of the cost of the loan to the borrower including interest or discount and expenses and charges for commission, brokerage, chattel mortgage and recording fees, inquiries, defaults, renewals, fines, penalties, or other similar costs, whether paid to or charged by the lender or paid to or charged by any other person, and whether
Central Finance Corporation

fixed and determined by the loan contract itself or in whole or in part by any other collateral contract or document by which the charges if any, imposed under the loan, contract or the terms of the repayment of the loan are effectively varied.
Therefore, "cost" is said to include two things which, in my opinion, ought to be differentiated. "Cost" is said to include, first, interest or discount and, second, the expenses and charges for commissions, brokerage, chattel mortgage and recording fees and the like. Roughly speaking, we can break up the definition of "cost" into two divisions, that portion which is purely interest and that portion which is not interest. For the purposes of this discussion we can describe that portion which is not interest as charges.
I am opposed to the principle of this bill for a number of reasons. Section 13 of the draft bill provides:
The Money-Lenders Act, chapter 135 of the
Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, is repealed.
My reasons for opposing the principles involved in the draft bill and in the bill now before the committee are these. The draft bill and the bill before the committee fix an interest rate of two per cent per month. It may be said that my statement in that respect is not correct, in that it is the cost of the loan that is fixed at two per cent per month. But I would point this out to hon. members of the committee. It would be open to money-lenders under this legislation to fix a rate of two per cent per month and call it all interest, and in that way this draft bill and the bill now before the committee authorize an interest rate of two per cent per month, which works out at the rate of approximately 26J per cent per annum. Now let us see the situation in which this parliament would be placed if we passed this bill or the draft bill recommended by the committee. At the present time we have,-I think I am correct in stating,-three general statutes that deal with the subject of interest. We have the Interest Act, which does not specify any rate of interest. It provides in its essence that in a written document the rate of interest shall be stated, and that if the rate of interest is not stated then the maximum which may be collected in interest shall be the legal rate of 5 per cent per annum. The second statute that we have dealing with interest and the interest rate is the Bank Act, in which a maximum of 7 per cent per annum is provided for. Then we have a third statute, the MoneyLenders Act, which provides for a maximum rate of interest of 12 per cent per annum for an extremely limited class of transactions.

The general bill and the private bill that is now before the committee propose that this maximum rate of 12 per cent per annum shall be increased to a maximum rate of two per cent per month, or an annual maximum rate of 26J per cent. Now, Mr. Chairman, when we are seeking in every possible manner to bring down the rate of interest-when we are seeking that by refunding our national debt as widely as we can at a lower rate of interest; when we are making provision for loans to municipalities under certain circumstances at a very low rate of interest; when we are making provision for assisting in the construction of houses at a very low rate of interest-there are many of us who feel that it would be psychologically wrong on the part of this parliament to raise the maximum rate that we have now of 12 per cent per annum to 26J per cent per annum.
It may well be argued that it is desirable to exercise certain controls over these moneylending companies, and, of course, it is desirable that we should exercise some control over them. With that object in view I suggested an amendment when the motion to adopt the preamble of the report was made. My amendment was as follows:
That that portion of the "cost" of a loan, as defined in section (2) paragraph (a) of the draft bill, which is interest, be fixed at a rate not exceeding 12 per centum per annum and that the right of any provincial legislature to reduce the remainder of the cost be preserved.
I proposed that amendment to the motion to adopt the preamble of the report for the following reasons. I thought it desirable that we should not exceed the maximum rate of interest that is now provided by the MoneyLenders Act. I thought it desirable also that we should seek to impose a limit on the total cost of a loan, but that we should leave the provinces free to deal with that portion of the cost of the loan which is not interest, in such a way as to reduce that portion of the cost. In other words, the suggestion which I made to the committee, and which a number of other members made, was this. We likened the proposed bill to a dwelling consisting of two storeys. The first storey was the interest storey of the dwelling. The second storey would be the charges storey of the dwelling. In other words, we proposed to erect a ceiling beyond which the loan companies would not be permitted to go in charging for the cost of the loan; but it was my view that we should not as a dominion parliament occupy the whole of the second storey, but that provincial jurisdiction to bring down the ceiling should be maintained

Central Finance Corporation
That landed us in a very long and somewhat involved argument as to the jurisdiction of this parliament to deal with the whole matter.
We had the opinion of a representative of the Department of Justice, Mr. Varcoe; we had also before us throughout the whole of our deliberations Mr. Finlayson, superintendent of insurance. While I am on the subject,
I am sure I state the views of every member of the committee on banking and commerce when I say that we were greatly indebted to these two officers for the assistance they gave to us. Indeed, Mr. Chairman, I think we are exceedingly fortunate in this country in having the type of public servant that we have. I do not think we sufficiently recognize their value and their devotion to their various departments and their duties. Mr. Varcoe, representing the Department of Justice, took the position that it was quite within the jurisdiction of the dominion parliament to pass the draft bill which we were then considering. He pointed out that the dominion had exclusive jurisdiction to deal with the subject of interest, and that our jurisdiction in respect of that matter could not be challenged. He also expressed the view that we had jurisdiction to pass this measure on the ground that the dominion had exclusive jurisdiction over the subject of criminal law; that the prohibition or suppression of usury was within the ambit of criminal law, and that our jurisdiction in respect of the matter from the point of view of enacting sound, valid criminal law was unquestionable. He also suggested that we had jurisdiction to deal with this subject on the ground that under section 91 of the British North America Act the dominion parliament has jurisdiction over trade and commerce. There was some controversy as to whether this was a sound ground on which to defend the dominion jurisdiction with respect to the matter.
So far there was not much dispute in the committee on the field of jurisdiction. But when we began to consider the definition section which I read at the opening of my remarks, namely the definition of cost, as it appears in the draft bill, there was great controversy. Representatives of a number of the provinces took the view that the dominion had no jurisdiction to deal with that portion of the cost of a loan which is not interest; that the dominion should confine itself to dealing with interest, and that the provinces should deal with that other portion of the cost of a loan which is not interest. On this subject Mr. Varcoe took the view, and a great many of us agreed with him, that the dominion did have jurisdiction to deal with the subject of costs and charges where they
are ancillary or necessarily incidental to the subject of interest, in considering what the total cost of a loan should be. I agreed that we did have jurisdiction, and I pointed out that in a number of cases the dominion parliament has jurisdiction to invade what would otherwise be the provincial field of jurisdiction, when that invasion is in respect of matters that are ancillary or necessarily incidental to some subject which clearly comes within dominion jurisdiction. The purpose of my amendment, however, was that we should not exercise this jurisdiction to invade the provincial field; that we should be careful about invasions of the provincial field of jurisdiction. The attorney general of Ontario took exception to our intended invasion. Representatives from the province of Quebec took a similar objection; and the proposed measure was offensive to a number of other provinces. It was with that in mind that I proposed the amendment which I have just set forth.
We had a twofold objection to the measure. In the first place many of us felt that this parliament should not stamp its approval of an interest rate of 26i per cent per annum on this bill. We felt that this was wrong, that it was contrary to the whole trend of legislation. Then we felt that we ought not to invade in an arbitrary manner the provincial field of jurisdiction. We therefore devised the amendment which I read a few moments ago, that we should not go any further in respect of our jurisdiction over interest, purely as such, than we have gone already in the Money-Lenders Act, and that consequently we should fix that portion of the cost of a loan which is purely interest at a maximum of 12 per cent per annum. We also felt that it was desirable to limit the total cost of the loan, which we did in this bill by fixing the total cost at two per cent per month. But we felt that we ought not to invade the provincial field of jurisdiction exclusively in such a way as to bar the provinces from legislating on the subject of charges. If the amendment which I suggested had carried, we would have accomplished these two purposes. We would have fixed a limit to the total cost of the loan to the borrower, but we would not have given the stamp of approval to an interest rate of 26J per cent.
Objection was taken to the amendment on the ground that it was not within the jurisdiction of this parliament, but I must confess that I could not understand the grounds of this objection. Unquestionably this parliament has jurisdiction to deal with the subject of interest. There is no dispute on that

Central Finance Corporation
question. If we have jurisdiction to deal with other subjects connected with the cost of a loan, such as recording fees, investigation charges and the like, then our jurisdiction to deal with such matters is only on the ground that these matters are ancillary or incidental to the subject of interest. If we have that jurisdiction, then I can see no reason why we should not exercise our jurisdiction with regard to .the subject matter of interest and leave the maximum interest rate exactly where it is now in the Money-Lenders Act. Under our jurisdiction over charges as being ancillary or necessarily incidental to interest we could fix a limit to the total cost of a loan. But in exercising our jurisdiction in that respect we need not do so to the exclusion of the provinces. We could leave the provinces perfectly free to deal in any way with the subjeot of charges on those loans, other than interest, so that the total of the charges could be brought down below the maximum rate of two per cent per month. That would have brought about the object which I think everyone is desirous of accomplishing, without giving our seal of approval to a maximum interest rate of 26J per cent per annum.
My point is this, that if we have jurisdiction to deal with .the subject of charges at all, as being part of the cost of a loan, we have jurisdiction to deal with the subject matter of charges; and we can deal with the subject matter of charges in any way we like. We do not have to deal with the subject matter of charges along with interest, but we may deal with interest separately and with charges separately.
The provinces of Ontario and Quebec raised objection to our proposed action. Why should we arbitrarily assert a jurisdiction in respect of these matters when these two great provinces object to our exercising that jurisdiction? Furthermore, in the province of Manitoba we have an act providing for the regulation under certain circumstances of money-lending transactions. If the proposed general bill were passed or if this private bill were passed, then it would not be competent for our courts in Manitoba for example to enforce the provincial act, because the dominion would have exercised its jurisdiction to invade what would otherwise be the provincial field of jurisdiction, and its legislation in the matter would override the provincial legislation. That was the controversy which took place in the committee on the question of jurisdiction.
As I pointed out a moment ago, the proposed draft bill is in two parts. Part I might be declared ultra vires by the courts on the ground that the dominion does not possess the jurisdiction which a number of us thought 	,
it did. It is possible that the representative of the Department of Justice and the other lawyers who argued in support of the dominion jurisdiction are wrong and that the court would declare that part I of the proposed general bill was ultra vires. For that reason part II would have to be considered. Part II, it is true, applies only to dominion companies. Whatever doubt there may be as to the validity of part I and the jurisdiction of parliament to pass part I, there can be no doubt whatsoever as to the jurisdiction of this parliament to pass part II, because this parliament has complete power to incorporate companies with objects that are not provincial. The power of incorporation is dealt with in the British North America Act in section 92. There the provincial power of incorporation is described, and my recollection of that provincial power is to this effect, that the province may incorporate companies for purposes that are provincial. It therefore follows, as a natural consequence, that the power to incorporate companies for purposes which are not provincial must, of necessity, reside with the dominion parliament. Therefore it is quite within our jurisdiction to impose any restrictions we like upon dominion companies. We can vest them with any power we see fit to give them, and can subject them to any limitations that we consider desirable; and if any criticism could be made of the amendment which I proposed in committee in respect of part I of the bill, no similar criticism can be made with respect to part II.

speechtext:
The bill relating to the Lord's Day Act, which passed this house a short time ago, was not recognizable upon its return from its journey to the senate; in fact there is nothing left of its original form or appearance except the number. It still bears number 13. I am not superstitious, but I am afraid my bill has been in bad company. I always thought an amendment meant the adding to or taking away from an original proposition of some sort. The senate has not amended my bill; it has simply substituted its own bill. To qualify properly the amendment of the senate, I wish to use the words of Senator Murdock: -I regard the amendment as merely a wooden gun with which to do some hunting. I think it is absolutely useless for the purpose of accomplishing what all honourable members of the committee desire, that is, to prevent unnecessary work on Sunday, which has prevailed in certain parts of the country.
I do not wish to be a party to such legislation. I refuse the amendment of the senate. It will serve no useful purpose. After all, if corporations, through their directors, violate the law, they should be punished; if they do not, I wonder why the senate is worrying so much about the possibility of gaol sentences.
Before resuming my seat I think it is my duty to thank this house for the support it gave my bill amending the Lord's Day Act.

Penitentiaries Commission Act

subtopic: INCORPORATION OF COMMISSION FOR ADMINISTRATION CONTROL AND MANAGEMENT-AMENDMENT OF EXISTING ACTS

speechtext:
The house resumed consideration in committee of the following resolution'-Mr. Lapointe (Quebec East)-Mr. Johnston (Lake Centre) in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to incorporate a commission with power under the Minister of Justice to administer, control and manage the penitentiaries; to provide for salaries of the commissioners and assistant commissioners and to amend and consolidate the Penitentiaries Act and amending acts and repeal the same.

subtopic: INCORPORATION OF COMMISSION FOR ADMINISTRATION CONTROL AND MANAGEMENT-AMENDMENT OF EXISTING ACTS
speechtext:
When the committee rose at six o'clock, Mr. Chairman, I was pointing out the necessity for the bill which the Minister of Justice proposes to introduce, providing for the appointment at a very early date of a governing commission for the penitentiaries, to consist, I believe, of three members. I was saying that it would be inviting trouble if we did not take action on the report of the royal commission. Even our fellow human beings in the penitentiaries know something of what is going on, and I think they would take such a step to mean that the report was not to be taken seriously. I am sure the government does intend to take it seriously, so I am most anxious that the minister should be allowed to proceed at once to introduce the bill.
The speaker who preceded me spoke of the need of having only one person rather than a commission in charge of prisons. The royal commission to investigate the penal system of Canada dealt with that very point at page 342 of their report, where they said:
In our present system the problem of penal administration is too large in scope and too serious in results to be left in the hands of one man. It is noteworthy, as a matter of record, that Canada is practically the only country where the penal system is not administered by some kind of commission or board.
So, when we appoint a commission of three to take care of our penitentiaries, we are following what has been done in other countries rather than breaking new ground. The important thing, of course, is the personnel of the commission. I feel quite sure that the Minister of Justice, who was instrumental in having the royal commission appointed, will .take very great care in choosing the personnel of the governing commission. They should have a vision of what can be done.

I want to say here that I do not think all the prisoners in our penal institutions can be made good citizens. I was delighted to see it stated in the report, which we shall have an opportunity to read more leisurely later on, that the commissioners realize that there are in our prisons incorrigible and intractable men whom it will never be safe to let out into society. They suggest that such men should never be allowed to mingle with their fellows. However, there are in our penitentiaries large numbers of prisoners who can be made responsible and respectable citizens. The commissioners to be appointed should be men of vision. They should be men who have a respect for human nature, even though it has gone astray. They should be men of character, and they should possess the training and culture necessary for such a job. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) is in the enviable position of being able to place in the hands of this commission the best text-book on penal matters, the report of the royal commission, that we have ever had in Canada. The report does not suggest that all the changes should be made hurriedly. In one place it states that the commissioners believe it will take at least five years to make all the suggested changes in the personnel of the penitentiaries which they consider are essential; and as a start, I do not think we can stress too much the importance of the personnel of the commission to be appointed.
Canadian penitentiaries are in great need of reform. In the report figures are quoted which must be familiar to all members of the house. It is stated that in the last eleven years there have been twenty disturbances in Canadian penal institutions, sixteen of these disturbances having taken place during the regime of the present superintendent, General Ormond. The report contains some interesting information in connection with recidivism. In 1935 there were per 100,000 of population, sixty recidivists having three or more convictions, and twenty-nine having two convictions. That rate is much higher than it has been in former years.
In the first pages of their report the commissioners point out that there are three great principles to be considered in penology. First, there is the prevention of crime through proper youth training and the providing of opportunities for youth. Second, there is the treatment of prisoners so that they will be fit to return to society. If it is found that they are not fit to be returned to society, then they should be kept in a special prison by themselves. Third, there is the rehabili-

Penitentiaries Commission Act
tion of the released prisoner. I do not want to take up too much time at this late period in the session, and there is no necessity to go into the many recommendations made by the commission. Some of these are extremely important. They believe in the Borstal system for the young offender. They believe in the classification of prisoners. They believe in the training of the officers who are to handle prisoners. They suggest that a training school should be set up and only officers who pass through that school should be put in charge of prisoners.
The royal commission was headed by Mr. Justice Joseph Archambault, the other members being Mr. R. W. Craig, K.C., at one time attorney general of Manitoba, and Mr. J. C. McRuer, K.C., of Toronto. That commission did a splendid work. I think Mr. Justice Joseph Archambault should be congratulated by every Canadian citizen upon the excellent work he did. He carried on his duties under a disadvantage. He suffered two serious injuries just before he commenced his work, and although his health was not too good during the time of the sittings of the commission, he performed his work in a most splendid way. I do not think anyone could appear before that commission without realizing the earnestness of Mr. Justice Joseph Archambault and the other two commissioners, They were not out gunning for anybody; they were out to find out all they could about the penitentiaries of Canada. Everyone had a chance to appear before them. The commission visited 113 institutions in nine countries and spent 108 days in seven Canadian penitentiaries taking the evidence of 1,084 inmates and 200 officers. Letters, briefs and manuscripts were received from 1,200 citizens, and in addition private and public hearings were held throughout Canada. Anyone who wanted to say anything about the penitentiaries of Canada had ample opportunity to do so.

Some of these people have had to resort to crime in order to get food and shelter. I do not intend to say any more except to stress my appreciation of the action of the government and the attitude of the Minister of Justice. The minister does not take any criticism of the penal system to be a personal affront. He takes it for what it is, a criticism of the system, and sets out to remedy an institution which he believes is outmoded, which stresses the punitive rather than the reformative side. The government are to be congratulated upon the appointment of such a splendid commission and in having this report ready at least by the end of the session. They are about to introduce a bill to provide for a prison board of three. I do not expect that all the recommendations made in this report will be put into effect immediately-it may be that some of them will never be put into effect-but I think it provides a blueprint which the commission of three to be appointed can follow in building up a system which, I am sure, will be much, better than the one we have.

subtopic: INCORPORATION OF COMMISSION FOR ADMINISTRATION CONTROL AND MANAGEMENT-AMENDMENT OF EXISTING ACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do
not claim to know very much about penitentiaries because I have never been a prisoner and1 have never made a special study of penology. However, as a member of this house and as a citizen of Canada I recognize the difficulty of the task that confronts the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and the government. I realize the extent of the work accomplished by this commission. They had to decide either to whitewash one of our institutions or else be as thorough as it was possible to be and let the chips fall where they may. I think the commission should be congratulated upon their thoroughness. The fact that they spent 108 days in Canadian penal institutions is an indication of the manner in which they went at their task. The editorials in one newspaper published in this city have been quite critical of the report, and other newspapers, although not very many, have adopted the same attitude, so I was not surprised to hear the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) say what he did this afternoon.
When I heard the leader of the opposition speak this afternoon of the prisons, the cells and the food, the paddles and so on, it made
Penitentiaries Commission Act

me think of the emphasis that we place on that man-made institution which we call the law. It. is an inanimate creature; but we emphasize it and miss the most important essential, the human values involved. I understand that the commission not only saw the prisons, the food and the cells, but that they spent time with the prisoners and saw discipline being administered to them. They recognized the human values that are involved in penology in this country as in any other.
We are too prone to emphasize the fact that these men are outcasts from society. That may be very true; but I happen to have in this country a very dear friend-and this is why I wanted to speak to-night very briefly -who through a mistake he made earlier in his life received a sentence of three years in one of our penitentiaries. He is now a respectable citizen and holds an excellent position, and from him I have learned a good deal of the truth of the material that is contained in the report of the Archambault commission. I wish to commend the idea of appointing a commission of three men to replace the present superintendency of the penitentiaries by one man. The responsibility is too great for any one man. Even a three-man commission may not be adequate to solve the root problems of human relationships that are there, but its appointment is a step in the direction which must be taken of removing the whole responsibility from one man. Suppose we conducted our penitentiaries from this angle: Is every lawbreaker in this country in gaol, or are the inmates criminals just because they happened to be caught? I sometimes think of reasons for gratitude that circumstances have been just a little different in my case from what they have been with some men that I know. It is very easy for any of us here to think of criminals as outcasts, that they have offended against society and so on, but we are not excused from giving them every care. I think the minister and the government and the commission are to be commended, and I congratulate the government upon the steps they are taking to implement the recommendations of the commission so far as they are able to implement them at this time.

subtopic: INCORPORATION OF COMMISSION FOR ADMINISTRATION CONTROL AND MANAGEMENT-AMENDMENT OF EXISTING ACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have one protest to lodge, not in regard to the report of the commission itself, but in regard to implementing the report in legislation at this stage of the session. It has been impossible for members of the house, attending its daily sittings and committee work, to give to the report, which was received only a few days ago, the consideration it deserves, and I think the minister would be well advised to accept

the suggestion which the leader of the opposition made this afternoon and postpone this legislation until next session. During the recess we would have an opportunity of studying the report, and then when we come back here we would be in a position to deal with the matter as it should be dealt with.
I notice that the press throughout the country takes a similar view. The Kingston Whig-Standard, for example, says, in part:
We have no idea what the government at Ottawa is going to do with the Archambault report. We hope they give it very serious consideration before they start putting its suggestions into effect. Many of the recommendations are doubtless of value, but many others should be carefully investigated before they are adopted. We hope that the evidence of 1,840 convicts will not weigh too heavily with Right Hon. Mackenzie King. And again we doubt very much whether honest and conscientious prison officials should be dismissed without being given a chance to reply to charges made against them.
And from the Brantford Expositor:
There is one phase of the royal commission's report on penitentiaries that Canadians will follow with considerable interest, and that is the recommendation for more lenient discipline on the part of the authorities. There is no desire to see the inmates of these institutions treated harshly or vindictively, but if it is to be a ease as to whether officials or the prisoners are going to run the penitentiaries there should be only one answer.
The class of men who fill the penitentiaries to a very great extent are sent there for grievous crimes against society, and many of them are hardened criminals who have been convicted many times. It is not to be supposed that these men are to be treated like guests at some palatial hotel. They should be given every opportunity to increase their education if they so desire and to become proficient in some of the technical crafts. They are entitled to kindly and humane treatment, together with facilities for recreation, but their term of imprisonment would be worthless if it did not impress upon them the absolute necessity of obedience to properly constituted authority. They go there as enemies of society and they should be taught that the rule of individual force cannot supplant the laws of the state . . .
In view of all that has happened the Hon. Ernest Lapointe, Minister of Justice, who is responsible for the administration of the penitentiaries throughout the dominion, will do well not to be too strongly influenced by the element that is at all times so clamorously urging the "coddling" of prisoners.
I do not intend to discuss the legislation, but I wish to urge upon the minister once more its importance. There is no doubt that he realizes it, and that those of us who represent people in all the different sections of Canada should at least have an opportunity to study the report further before being called upon to deal with it in legislation. What

Penitentiaries Commission Act
difference would postponing the legislation for a few months make? We have carried on with the present administration of the penitentiaries under the present Minister of Justice for three years and have heard no complaint, and therefore I think there would be no great hardship in continuing with the present administration for a few months longer until legislation can be brought down in proper shape at the next session of parliament.

subtopic: INCORPORATION OF COMMISSION FOR ADMINISTRATION CONTROL AND MANAGEMENT-AMENDMENT OF EXISTING ACTS
speechtext:
I merely wish to ask a question of the right hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). Is it the government's intention to appoint a physician to the commission the institution of which is recommended in the royal commission's report? In my opinion, one of the members of this commission should be a physician specially versed in criminology.
I think the Minister will agree with me that penitentiary, administration is not simply a question of economy and discipline, but that the mental condition of the inmates must also be considered. The appointment to this commission of a physician who would make a special study of the general health and mentality of the prisoners seems to me indispensable. Many crimes can be attributed! to mental derangement. A physician versed in criminology could render useful service in penitentiary administration, not only as regards the physical health of the inmates but also their moral rehabilitation, so that at the expiration of their sentence they may return to normal life and contribute to the development of the country.

subtopic: INCORPORATION OF COMMISSION FOR ADMINISTRATION CONTROL AND MANAGEMENT-AMENDMENT OF EXISTING ACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to speak at any great length. In view of the fact, however, that St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary is situated in my constituency, I deem it my duty to offer a few observations.
On April 15th, 1936, Lieut. Col. Piuze, a former warden of St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary, forwarded to the Superintendent of Penitentiaries at Ottawa a report on penitentiary administration, on the training of youthful prisoners and on the International Prison Congress. This report contains highly interesting suggestions and recommendations. May I refer hon. members to the ex-warden's findings on pages 22 and 23 and to his recommendations on pages 65 , 66, 67, 68 and 69, which I shall quote, in order that they may appear in Hansard-. On pages 22 and 23 of his report, Lieut. Col. Piuze states the following findings:
(Text) In the four countries I visited, I would have been anxious to take advantage of numerous offers I received to make a study of
other institutions specially destined to the confinement and reformation of young delinquents. It would have afforded me the opportunity to substantially increase the knowledge I have gained and would have permitted me to submit a much more thorough report. Unfortunately the limited time at my disposal prevented me from so doing.
In my humble opinion the Borstal system with certain modifications is the most adaptable for this country. However, it would not be possible for the time being at least to introduce it outright in view of the territorial conditions and also in consideration of the lack of adequate accommodation.
For the present I think that the best solution would be to hasten the construction of Laval buildings at St. Vincent de Paul, Quebec, and of Collins Bay, at Kingston, Ontario, where young delinquents could be accommodated. Laval buildings could take care of the youths of the province of Quebec and of the maritimes; Collins Bay could accommodate those of Ontario and of the western provinces.
To obtain satisfactory results, it is of the utmost importance that the lads be entirely separated from older prisoners, and that there be no contact whatsoever with the latter. Until such a time as the two institutions already mentioned are ready for occupation, a certain segregation could be made in our penitentiaries, but only as a temporary measure. Even then, there will always be the "atmosphere" and possibility of contact with others.
It is my opinion that the only thing that could be done, until an appropriate accommodation is available, would be to assemble those young delinquents in separate cell blocks, giving them physical training, outdoor work, school work, and lectures. Later on when new quarters are ready, a more appropriate program of training could be devised.
I am not in favour of dormitories for young convicts, as they exist in the majority of Borstal institutions. Individual cubicles are much more reeommendable.
I would not, either, recommend too many recreations, and a well balanced discipline should be maintained. I do not feel inclined to recommend, either, that young convicts be granted more privileges than are afforded honest average youths outside.
As previously stated, the principle of the English Borstal system is very good, but I could not recommend all that is being done in England. Besides, local conditions are not the same, and the class of young delinquents here is also quite different from the type of lads in England, where they have to deal with English boys only, whereas in Canada, we have to take care of a much more cosmopolitan population.
Also it would not be possible, for some time at least, to classify these lads the way it is done in England, and this, owing to our wide territories and the relatively small distribution by provinces. Most of the English system could be introduced in this country when proper accommodation is available, and this system could be arranged so as to meet with our requirements.
(Signed) P. A. Piuze,
Warden.

(Translation) As to 'his recommendations, Mr. Chairman, they are to be found on pages 65, 66, 67, 68 and 69. They are as follows: Conclusions
(Text) The study tour of the different penal institutions visited has been most instructive and interesting to me, and I am most grateful to the authorities for having afforded me the opportunity of acquiring such an experience.
Observations
The few observations I intend to make, as a result of this study tour, will mostly apply to penitentiaries or convict prisons, this subject being more familiar to me.
The problems that penal administrators in Europe are confronted with are substantially different from ours. They are benefiting by a much longer and wider experience; territorial conditions are quite different.

speechtext: From what document is the hon. member quoting?

subtopic: INCORPORATION OF COMMISSION FOR ADMINISTRATION CONTROL AND MANAGEMENT-AMENDMENT OF EXISTING ACTS
speechtext:
From the report of the former warden of St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary.
They are dealing with their own countrymen; and finally, the class of criminals is not at all the same.
In the old country, and specially in England, prisoners, generally speaking, are well classified, and there are separate institutions for each class of offenders. For instance, there are distinct institutions for the young and first offenders; for recidivists and hardened criminals. Also, in view of the proximity of the various institutions, transfers, when necessary, can easily be effected without incurring much expense.
Comparisons
Shops. In our Canadian penitentiaries, favourable comparison can be made with European institutions, with regard to industries and teaching of trades. Our different workshops are much more modernly equipped, and a convict who is willing to learn a trade has full opportunity to do it.
Library. Our school and library departments are well organized, and full facilities are given to convicts to gain an elementary instruction, if illiterates, and to improve their degree of instruction, if the latter has been restricted to the elements of reading and writing.
Discipline. Although working under more difficult conditions, our discipline is good and well observed.
Construction. New construction is done by convict labour, while in European countries, such construction is mostly done by public works departments.
Humanization. As far as humanization is concerned, we compare favourably with other countries.
Diet. The feeding of convicts in our penal institutions is much superior; as a matter of fact, we are perhaps doing too much in that respect. We lack uniformity in our different penitentiaries; in each country in Europe, a diet is established and applied to all institutions, without exception.
Privileges. In certain countries, privileges are very limited, and in this regard, it is con-
[Mr. Lacombe.l	*
sidered that the English system is the most adequate. Prisoners are graded, and privileges may be enjoyed when stages have been reached. In other words, to receive privileges, prisoners must earn them by their good conduct, industry and dispositions. Having in view the procedure adopted and followed in European countries, it would appear that, in this country, privileges are allowed too soon after admission, and may not, therefore, be appreciated at their just value. It would seem more appropriate if authorized privileges were given when convicts have reached certain stages, and it is recommended that, during the probation at least- that is to say, during the first six months of incarceration-no privileges whatsoever, with the exception of library books, should be granted to convicts.
Classification. With our present system, young and first offenders, recidivists and hardened criminals all receive the same treatment, upon admission in our penitentiaries. It is of the utmost importance that classification of convicts be commenced as soon as possible, when proper accommodation is made available.
Recidivists. With our present penal system, recidivists and hardened criminals seem to scoff at our penitentiaries. Penitentiary life to them is such that, as soon as liberated, they resume their criminal activities. If they can manage to foil justice, well and good; but if caught again, they return with a feeling of relief, if one considers that, in one institution at least, approximately one-half of the population is made up of this class of criminals.
Cells. Our cellular system, with barrier doors, is most unsatisfactory, in many respects. It renders supervision very difficult, and ill-disposed convicts are at liberty to exercise their pernicious influence over others during talking periods.
Conversations. Conversations carried on in cells, during authorized hours, are far from being edifying. Their main subjects are immoralities, besides convicts boasting of their criminal exploits and criticizing the rules and regulations and the authorities. Well-disposed convicts must necessarily stand such conversations, which are permitted when the prison is closed, and when only a limited number of officers are on duty. At such times, proper control and supervision are 'well nigh impossible, and naturally, full advantage of the situation is taken by ill-intentioned convicts. One cannot imagine all the harm these badly-disposed convicts exercise over others who, in too many cases, leave the institution, on liberation, worse off morally than at the time they came in. In European institutions, conversations between convicts are tolerated during working periods only, it being the view that such conversations should not be more and need not be less than the conversations which take place amongst work people in properly managed workshops, that is to say, such remarks as the work required may cause, but there is no idle talking on general subjects.
Recommendations.	.
Classification. As far as St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary is concerned, classification of various classes of convicts could be started, as soon as the construction of Laval buildings is sufficiently advanced to allow occupancy. In this connection it is strongly recommended that the necessary buildings be constructed as soon

Penitentiaries Commission Act
as possible, subject to be completed. The question of adequate and additional accommodation for the exceptionally large population of this institution has 'been a long-felt need, and presently St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary is overcrowded, particularly the work shops, where twice as many convicts are put to work as should normally be employed in those departments.
The following scheme which might also be applicable to other institutions in this country is recommended:-
That St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary be used exclusively for recidivists and hardened criminals. The following shops could be reserved for this class of convicts; stonecutting, stonecrushing, machine and blacksmithing and other works in connection with the administration of the institution;
That Laval buildings be made two distinct prisons, divided by a central wall;
That one part of these buildings be reserved for first offenders who would be taught the following trades: tailoring, shoemaking, bookbinding, laundering, farming, electricity and motor mechanics;
That the other half of the buildings be used for young convicts between sixteen and twenty-one years of age, who would be physically trained, provided with outdoor work (gardening and construction) and education, (school attendance and lectures).
This classification, under one direction, would be something similar to what the writer has witnessed in Les Prisons de Fresnes, in France, and which, in his opinion, would meet the situation very well. Each of these establishments would be subjected to a distinct regime; in each, young and first offenders, recidivists and hardened criminals, would be graded according to their crime, sentence, antecedents, capacity and merits, and wrould be entitled to appropriate privileges.
This system would assure constructive reformation work, and would protect the young and first offenders from contact with, and the bad influence of, recidivists and hardened criminals.
Special treatment for recidivists and hardened criminals would no doubt result in a sensible reduction in our penitentiaries of this class of convicts. At present, their percentage is out of all normal proportions, when compared with similar types, in European countries.
Cells. In the old country, all penal institutions have the "closed door" cell system, with cells on each side and a wide corridor in the centre, lighted by means of skylights in roofs.
It is strongly recommended that all cell blocks at Laval buildings, and other similar new construction, be made on the "closed door" principle. It would not be possible, for the present at least, and in view of the expense it would incur, to remodel our existing cell blocks as suggested above; but to remedy the situation, it is recommended that all wings be closed by means of concrete walls, instead of barriers, and that the floors of each range be extended to the wall, thus segregating each wing, and even each range. This could be done at comparatively low cost.
Silence rule. It is recommended that silence rules be restored in cell blocks, and this, in the best interests of administration, discipline and security.
Punishment cells. Our system of prisons of isolation, (punishment cells) could be very much improved upon, and we could advantageously adopt the same system as used, for instance, in English prisons, which is far superior to ours, and in the writer's opinion, the only adequate one.
Agitators and badly disposed convicts. It is a well known fact that certain convicts, with very bad character and dispositions, and known as trouble makers, are the leaders in riots and disturbances, and also that, in the majority of cases, are responsible, directly or indirectly, for damages caused to government property.
It is suggested that such class of convicts, from all penitentiaries, be congregated in a separate institution, where they would be subjected to special discipline and treatment; if eliminated from other institutions, they would not have the opportunity to exercise their pernicious influence over other convicts.
Superior officers. Wardens and deputy wardens are entitled to twenty-one days annual leave, and in that respect, do not receive any more consideration than a prison guard, notwithstanding their numerous and heavy responsibilities and standing. It is pointed out that, in England for instance, governors and deputy governors are entitled to six weeks annual leave, while the other members of the staffs receive three weeks of such leave.
It has been noticed, in the various institutions visited, that a difference exists in uniforms for officers of higher grades, distinguishing superior officers from other ranks. A similar distinction, in the Canadian institutions, is recommended for consideration.
Officers' quarters. In countries visited, all permanent officers are given free quarters. If this privilege could be afforded our penitentiary officers, the service would certainly benefit by it, in that sense that all the members of the personnel would reside at proximity of the institution, thus assuring better security, and furthermore, this would be an additional inducement for officers to hold on to their positions, and no doubt would result in better service and more devotion to duty. With such additional consideration, officers would certainly better appreciate their positions.
Training schools. It is recommended that a training school be established for penitentiary officers, as it exists in European countries.
The service generally would certainly benefit greatly by such an innovation, and candidates, when called for duty, would have received both theoretical and practical training.
Such a school could be established in one of our penitentiaries, and its functioning would entail very little expense.
The above suggestions and recommendations are respectfully submitted, having in view the betterment of the service, and the reforms suggested are considered to be in the best interest of the administration and management of penal institutions, and the treatment of convicts as a whole.
That is signed by E. A. Piuze, the then warden.
(Translation) In conclusion, I wish to quote the 12th recommendation on page 355 of the

Penitentiaries Commission Act
report of the Royal Commission on the Penal System of Canada, thus:
The pay of officers should he brought up to a reasonable standard, having regard to the type of service performed.
I also wish to take this opportunity to ask, not only that penitentiary guards and officers be paid a reasonable salary, but that they be paid fortnightly, as are other civil employees of Canada, instead of monthly.
The Minister of Justice will perhaps tell me that such a measure would require an army of accountants. Then, I would say to the minister: Open the doors wide particularly in my district, to the graduates of the School of Higher Commercial Studies. If seven or eight additional accountants are employed, that' would 'be just another way to relieve unemployment. We have really sad cases in St. Vincent de Paul where fathers of twelve, or thirteen children must wait for their salary till the end of the month in order to pay their grocery and other bills. I ask the minister to grant this very humane request. On the other hand, in the public interest and in the interest of our penal institutions, I think that military discipline on Sundays should be abolished in all our penitentiaries.
Mr. Chairman, the royal commission has severely criticized the former warden of St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary for having instituted military discipline in the penitentiary in mry constituency. That is the reason why I akk the Minister of Justice to abolish, not only in that penitentiary, but in all other such institutions of Canada, Sunday discipline which is absolutely unnecessary, may I add, because there is ample time, on week days, to give the inmates all the physical exercise they require.
Before I resume my seat, I want to say that the recommendations and findings of Lieut. Col. P. A. Piuze are generally in accord with those of the royal commission on the penal system of Canada, except as to the establishment of the Borstal system in this country. In fact, according to Lieut. Col. P. A. Piuze, that system cannot be fully applied in Canada. In view of his plausible arguments, I think his opinion should prevail.
As a matter of fact, Lieut. Col. Piuze has been warden of St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary for six years, and I wish to tell this house that he has adequately filled that position and that he possesses unequalled experience. Recognized authorities of this country have told me personally that he could not be easily replaced. I do not wish, Mr. Chairman, to make a case for Lieut Col. Piuze tonight. However, I am free to state to this

house that Lieut. Col. Piuze, in his report, has submitted to the Canadian government recommendations and suggestions of a highly practical nature, which would be very easy to apply, and I have no comparison to make with the report of the royal commission on penitentiaries.

speechtext:
At this very late
date in the session, Mr. Chairman, it is not my purpose to discuss the question of penal reform or to go in any detail into the report upon which this resolution is founded, but I should like to endorse the general position taken by the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Miss Macphail) with regard to this question and to express my appreciation of the fact that although it is so late in the session the government apparently has considered it possible to bring forward legislation of this kind. The hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Barber) quoted an editorial opposed to action along this line. I hold in my hand a whole sheaf of editorials from the leading newspapers of this country, all of them favourable to action along the line proposed.
I should like to protest against the position taken by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), first of all in regard to his attitude toward the prisoners. He asserted that they were the victims of their own wrong-doing. That is only partly true. I think it may be said that the larger number were the victims of the neglect of society. I do not want to go into that question at any length, but I think it is conceded that a very large number of our criminals would have gone straight if they had had half a chance. I remember when I was only a youth reading Jean Valjean, that immortal work of Victor Hugo, which no doubt many other hon. members also read. You will remember the way in which that great French writer interested us in the criminal, and I have never gotten away from his presentation of a man who, according to the category of the right hon. leader of the opposition, 1 suppose would be classed as a mad dog running wild. I object to that way of viewing the criminal. There may be some criminals who are mad dogs running wild, who have to be dealt with more or less, as we might deal with a dangerous animal, but the majority are not of that class.
Then I think of some who, in spite of the bad treatment we have given them, have reformed. I think of one man in my own city of Winnipeg whose family I know very well. He robbed a post office when he was a boy, was imprisoned and later released. To-day he occupies one of the most important

Penitentiaries Commission Act
positions in that city, and I suppose only a few old-timers remember that he once served a penitentiary sentence. I feel indignant when I think of him being classed as a mad dog running wild.
I do not think the leader of the opposition was quite fair to the commission when he spoke of them as listening to the tittle-tattle of convicts. If they were to get information, why should they not listen to the men who were incarcerated in the penitentiaries, even though they were branded as convicts? I should think it probable they could get a great deal more information from listening to those who were enduring the abuses than by listening to the officials who may be seeking to paint as rosy a picture as possible. However, I shall not go into this phase of the question to-night.
I want to protest against any further delay in dealing with this matter. Some of the older members of the house will recall that four years ago, on June 30, we considered this question of penitentiaries. This matter had been put off and off until what was hoped would be the last day of the session. The hon. member for Grey-Bruce made a strong appeal to the then Minister of Justice, Mr. Guthrie, to take action. The minister replied that it was too late in the session; that the Governor General was then on his way to prorogue parliament, it being then within a few minutes of twelve o'clock on Saturday night. We could not sit on Sunday, and Monday was a holiday. I do not know whether I should boast of it, but on that occasion I said that the estimate under discussion would not pass. I succeeded in holding up the house, and hon. members had to remain here on Sunday and Monday and sit again on Tuesday, when we considered this matter of penitentiary reform. I should like to quote one paragraph of what I said at that time:
I would point out that the prisoners are the most defenceless class in the community. They have been deprived of the ordinary rights of citizenship. They have no means of making their grievances known to this house. They have been deprived of the rights of normal ordinary human beings.
But on the other hand I am coming to believe that we must discount to a considerable extent the official statements, the official denials, because it seems to have been the policy more or less to whitewash under-officials.
Furthermore, we urge that the time has come when there should be general consideration _ of the whole question of prison administration and the treatment of criminals.
I then urged the setting up of a commission. That was on June 30, 1934. That commission was set up, and I regret as much as anyone that its report has been presented so late in 51952-276
the session. However, we are glad finally to get this report. It is four years since these evils were definitely brought to the attention of the house. It will be remembered that at that time riots had occurred in Kingston penitentiary, and there had been shooting into the cell of one of the prisoners. It was an outrageous situation. We have the report of this commission, and now the leader of the opposition tells us that we ought to postpone action until we have had time to study the report. I am sorry the right hon. gentleman is not in the chamber, but I am sure that he must have given a considerable amount of study to penitentiary reform. Even the man on the street knows that reforms such as proposed are long overdue.
I submit that parliament should not prorogue without passing the remedial legislation to be based upon this resolution. Without disparaging the Conservative convention which is to take place next week, may I say I am not so sure but that this matter which is so vital to the thousands of people in our penitentiaries is not of as great importance. In any case it ought to be dealt with at this session.
I shall not go into the question raised by the leader of the opposition as to whether this is the best manner of dealing with General Ormond. The authorities can deal with him as they please, but what we do need is legislation. The gentlemen who composed this commission spent a long time in the most painstaking investigation. They travelled across Canada, in the United States and abroad in order to study the situation from all angles. I think they were in a better position to make recommendations than even hon. members who may have casually read this report and who might possibly be inclined to consider it in some of its political aspects. I urge the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) to let nothing stand in the way of bringing about these reforms without any further delay.

subtopic: INCORPORATION OF COMMISSION FOR ADMINISTRATION CONTROL AND MANAGEMENT-AMENDMENT OF EXISTING ACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I find myself just as displeased with the action of the government as my hon. friend is pleased. They have brought down this report very late in the session and have expected us to deal with it. It is almost two and a half years ago that the government appointed this royal commission to examine into this matter and report. Three months ago the report came into the hands of the minister, and fourteen days ago it was laid on the table of the house. Hon. members have had thirteen days in which to endeavour to inform themselves of the contents of the 400 pages comprising this report. After sitting here for five months I believe that the mind of the ordinary member is somewhat weary. He sits on com-

Penitentiaries Commission Act

mittees; he sits in the house; he deals with his correspondence and carries on the other work of a member. I, for one, have not had time more than to glance cursorily through this most important report. I do not think it is reasonable to expect us to deal with this matter at this late stage of the session.
I cannot go into the principle of the bill, because the only vision we have had of it is what is contained in the resolution. It does not seem to me to be fair to a civil servant of Canada to accept the recommendation of a commission in this regard, as apparently the government has done. The commission state that they were dissatisfied with their examination of the superintendent, and they recommend his dismissal. This afternoon my right hon. leader (Mr. Bennett) pointed out how the superintendent was appointed. Many people may have thought that the superintendent was appointed on the recommendation of the previous administration and, that, therefore, there may have been some partisan politics mixed up with the appointment. However, I believe that belief will be dispelled when attention is drawn to the important positions held by the six members of the committee appointed by the civil service commission to choose the superintendent.
We have not had time to give due consideration to a report on so important a matter. To dismiss a civil servant in this cursory way is not good for the civil service, and consequently is not good for Canada. It matters not to me whether he be a civil servant in the higher or lower ranks of the civil service ; the fact of the matter is that the investigation carried on by the commission has not been of such a nature as to warrant the recommendation made. It is noticeable, for instance, in the pages which deal briefly with the recommendations, that in this country, of course, every penal institution was visited, and at those institutions nine convicts were heard for every one official. The commission paid a visit to the United States and there examined the penal institutions and listened to the views expressed by the officials. The commission also visited the United Kingdom where they did likewise. But we are not aware that on their travels abroad the commissioners listened to any views of the convicts in those institutions. It appears to me from the cursory study that I have been able to make of this report that the commission has given an overweight of interest to the evidence of convicts in the Canadian penal institutions, and perhaps not sufficient weight to some of the other evidence.
I am not acquainted with the superintendent of penitentiaries. So far as I am aware, the

only time I ever saw him was when he sat before the Minister of Justice in the late administration when he was dealing with the estimates of that department, but I know his record. I know that he was a district officer commanding in the west. I know that if he had not moved over to this civil service job, other rungs of the ladder in the service would have been open to him, but it is hardly likely that those rungs will still be open to the superintendent if he leaves the civil service with such a smirch on his name. I earnestly appeal to the minister that at this late stage of the session it might be well to wait just that number of months longer which would enable us to give further consideration to this weighty report.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: INCORPORATION OF COMMISSION FOR ADMINISTRATION CONTROL AND MANAGEMENT-AMENDMENT OF EXISTING ACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not minimize, the committee may be sure, the great importance of this resolution and the legislation which will follow it. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) said, this question is one which has been before the country for many years. Rightly or wrongly there has been a feeling that all was not perhaps as well as it should be in the penal institutions of Canada, and I well remember well-meaning citizens imploring us to carry on an investigation. I was on the other side of the house at the time when that great social worker, my own fellow citizen and townsman, Archdeacon Scott, the padre, came to see me and besought me to plead with the then government for an investigation into the penitentiaries. A large body of public opinion was certainly aroused at the time, and when the campaign of 1935 took place the present leader of the government made a promise that there would be an investigation by royal commission into the administration of the penitentiaries.
We came into office in October, 1935, and the royal commission was appointed in February, 1936. The resolution before us is the result of the report of that commission. Whatever may be our opinion as to its findings and recommendations, I think everyone will agree that its report is a considerable and well-prepared work and that the commissioners have devoted their energies and abilities to doing the work as completely and even as perfectly as it could be done. This does not mean, of course, that we are to agree with everything they may suggest or recommend. I personally agree with a great many of the things they recommend. With some of them I do not agree, and as to many others I have doubts whether they should be carried into practice. But as far as one of the recommendations is concerned, and it is their main recommendation, the one which is embodied in

Penitentiaries Commission Act
this resolution and in the bill to follow, namely, the appointment of a commission or a prison board to replace the present administration, with that recommendation I am in agreement.
Most of the other suggestions and recommendations-and there is a multitude of them -will have to wait. Most of them can be carried out by regulations after the commission, the prison board, to be appointed will have satisfied themselves that they should be carried out; but the most important of them will have to be the subject of legislation, and parliament of course will have ample time to study the report and consider the advisability of making those changes. The commissioners in their report suggest that it is a work of five years to put into effect all the recommendations which they make, but this bill, I repeat, is merely for the purpose of creating a prison board.
I fully sympathize with the view expressed by my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), by my hon. friend the member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Barber), and by my hon. friend the member for Yale (Mr. Stirling), that the members of the house have not had sufficient time to read and consider this voluminous report; and if this legislation would have the effect of carrying out all the recommendations of the commission, I would certainly feel that their contention was even stronger than it is. But so far as merely creating a prison board is concerned, changing the present system in that respect, I do not see that it is so essential or necessary to have read all the arguments in favour of the numerous changes which are suggested. There may be some who think, as my right hon. friend does, that we should wait, but I am quite sure that there are a good many more who would strongly criticize the government for not doing anything this session after this report has been tabled.
I do not agree with the basis on which my right hon. friend lays his strongest objection. He says that we are asking the committee to render a verdict against General Ormond. We are doing nothing of the kind. It is not the person of the superintendent; it is the system against which a verdict is rendered. If there is a verdict it is a verdict against a system; it is a question not of changing a man and putting another man in his place, but of changing the system. My hon. friends who spoke of the dismissal of General Ormond did not state the position correctly. There is no question of dismissing the superintendent by the creation of a commission.

True, his office would disappear. As this happens quite frequently in the civil service, he would be eligible for retirement allowance if he is entitled to any. The question of dismissing General Ormond has not been considered at all. Surely, if the policy of having a prison board in charge of the administration of the penitentiaries of Canada is the right policy, no single man should be an obstacle to putting that policy into effect. I repeat, the fact of giving effect to the recommendation of creating a prison board does not mean that anything is done against the superintendent who is in charge at the present time.
Of course I would be following the line of least resistance if I were to accept the view that it would be better to wait a few months. This will be a very difficult task. The appointment of the three men who will serve on this prison board will be a task of great magnitude. Some seem to believe that we should find supermen for that work. Unfortunately they do not exist any more in Canada and the other countries of the world. We have to find the best men possible. I am free to admit that at the present time I do not know what men will be appointed on that board. I have already received many requests, and I am afraid I shall disappoint some of the writers when I say that the choice which will be made will not be made from among those who have written. I may add that these will not be political appointments. If there is a work which will be most responsible and difficult, it will be this. It is a work which does not bring much satisfaction. There is no occupation more open to criticism than that of those in charge of penitentiaries, working all the time earnestly, satisfying nobody and being subject to criticism which is not always fair. I think I am right in saying this. But I am going to do my best, with the help of my colleagues, to find three men who will most adequately recommend themselves to our appreciation. I have a great deal of sympathy with the suggestion of the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Gauthier) that one of them should be a medical man. I believe that is recommended by the members of the royal commission. But as hon. members will see when the bill is introduced, it will come into force only on proclamation. Of course we have to consolidate the Penitentiaries Act by striking out in many places the words "minister" and "superintendent" and replacing them by "board" or "commissioners." But the bill in itself will mainly consist of this great change of creating a 'board to administer the penitentiaries.

My right hon. friend has spoken of the parole system and of the change which is suggested by the commission. I must say, without enlarging upon it, that I am inclined to agree with him that the carrying out of the recommendation in that regard will be a difficult step to take. I do not think I have anything to add to this. When the bill is discussed after it has been introduced, I shall be prepared to give any further information.
