No, Mr. Chairman. The very moderate and fair statement of the minister commends itself, I think, to every member of the committee. But it does not meet what I conceive to be the real difficulty.
On the fourteenth day of June this report was filed. To-day is the twenty-eighth. The report is dated in April. Between April and June time was spent in printing it and, I take it, in translating it. We first saw it when it was tabled on June 14. That is only two weeks ago. I say frankly to the minister that although he deals with only one phase of the question, that affects the whole principle of prison administration in this country. If, for instance, one refers to matters in this report and points out that they are absolutely unwarranted in fact one draws the conclusion. I think properly, that little importance attaches to the whole. Take, for example, the attack against the firm of Morris, who sold coal. I mentioned that this afternoon, and I observed that in a letter written by John Morris to the newspaper he pointed out that the facts are exactly the opposite to those which are stated. With respect to Sowards it is quite clear that the same situation develops.
Take the Buck incident. I say to the minister that the reason why one approaches this matter with such a desire to read1 this report is that all you have to do is to consider the incident with respect to Buck. Wrho empowered these three men to sit as a court of appeal on Craig and the other commissioner who reported on the Buck incident at the time it happened? And what do these three men find? The minister knows what they found. They said that the reports which were made by the commissioners who investigated the matter at the request of the Minister of Justice arrived at conclusions that were wholly unwarranted. They refer to the fact that certain of these people were not experts in penology. But which one of the three royal

commissioners was? Was Craig? Was McRuer? Was Judge Archambault? These are not experts; yet they project themselves into this picture as experts; and now the government asks us to consent to changing the whole system of the administration of prisons in this country, although we have had this report before us for no more than two weeks. And the difficulty is that when the change is made it is not easy to undo it. The minister says he proposes that the bill will come into force on proclamation. I desire to point out to him that if this change is made, it will be possible to alter it only by act of parliament. Once we have committed ourselves to this scheme or plan, we shall have made it impossible to alter it except by statute.
Despite what the minister has said, the appointments will be political. I was pleased, indeed, to hear him say that he did1 not propose that they should be partisan political appointments, but the fact remains that they will be political appointments. It is contemplated that they should be. How did Ormond come into the picture? He came in through the civil service commission and through that board the names of which I gave this afternoon, who made the investigation they did and reported in his favour. The majority of the men who made that report were certainly not supporters of the administration by whom the appointment was made, and they took a great deal of time to consider the matter. Finally they recommended Ormond. They recommended his appointment because they believed that he was the best of the many applicants who offered. Men like Mr. Biggar, or Doctor Porteous, or Mr. Edwards, or Mr. Dufresne, or Colonel Kemmis, or the late Major-General Mac-Brien spent a great deal of time over the matter.
Now the government must make the appointments, and they are already confronted with a situation which I regard as intolerable. I agree with the minister in that respect. After to-day's debate he will be receiving letters from every part of this country, from men who think they have a claim, and there is not a member of this house supporting the administration who will not receive a communication in these terms, "Speak a good word to the Minister of Justice about my appointment." I went through such an experience in connection with the Bank of Canada, and the minister will now have the same experience. Before that, the civil service commission acted, and they regarded their duty as so serious that they appointed this committee, with the government, to choose General Ormond. I recalled this afternoon vividly

Penitentiaries Commission Act
how hard they had worked at it. They took a long time going over the applications, and it relieved us of much responsibility. The Minister of Justice of that day was able to say, "I had nothing to do with it." I was able to say, "I have nothing to do with it." The Minister of Justice will now be literally beseiged with applications for the position, and members supporting the administration will be in the same position. The appointments will therefore be political. I repeat, I am happy to hear the minister say that they will not be partisan political appointments, but they will be political appointments.
How does that compare with the civil service appointment? How does that compare with the recommendation made by the late Major-General MacBrien and those other gentlemen to whom I have referred? What about the pressure that will be brought to bear as compared with the situation where men make a recommendation after investigating thoroughly the records of the persons concerned? Perhaps the minister has overlooked the exact words of the report with respect to General Ormond:
Your commissioners are of the opinion that it is necessary to the good management of the penitentiary service that the superintendent should immediately be retired, and they recommend accordingly.	,
They had no power to do that; that was not the term of General Ormond's employment. He was not told that charges had been formulated against him, and he had no opportunity to be heard. Reading the report, one can see pretty well that it was not written by Judge Archambault, because there is nothing judicial about it. They take a sentence here and a question there, and the answer given by General Ormond. He was eight days before them although he had not a chance to meet these people who gave evidence against him. He was eight days being grilled by these three men, all three lawyers, he himself having been a soldier; and they pick out an answer he gave and then make a recommendation. And the recommendation is that he should be immediately retired. That is not fair. The minister says, "We are not going to retire him", but the minute you substitute this board for the superintendent, that minute he goes out of office. It is not fair that a royal commission should so recommend when a man is employed as General Ormond was. What happened? Without formulating charges against him, without saying what the charges against him were, in order that he might specifically meet them, he is dragged into a room and kept for eight days, not being
present when these people were making the case against him. And who were the men that made cases against him? Outcasts of society. One of my hon. friends says, "Oh, well, these poor fellows would not have been so bad if they had had a chance." But I was glad to hear the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Miss Macphail) say to-night that there are in-corrigibles in penitentiaries. That is an improvement on what used to be said.

That statement is made five years afterwards. They continue:
When the superintendent-
This is our poor friend who came into the service in this way:
-had become acquainted with these circumstances he ought to have instigated an immediate and thorough investigation to determine the names of the men who had fired the shots, and this investigation should have been pursued with as much diligence as the investigation of any other crime.
The militia was outside, having been called in, and it was not apparent whether the shots had been fired by the prison warders or by the militia. He should have seen to it which man fired that shot! That is what these men report. I ask any hon. member what he thinks of that.
(5)	When Mr. Buckley's complaint was received, in August, 1933, the inspectors were instructed to conduct an investigation because there was no record of any appropriate investigation having taken place.
(6)	The investigation by Inspectors Craig and Dawson was not carried out with the efficiency the circumstances warranted.
And the commissioners made their report. They said that there he was, in D tier, the top, I went and saw it myself and saw the marks of the shots. They said that these men fired at such an angle as to endeavour to strike
Penitentiaries Commission Act

the ceiling, but, this being the top tier, some shots struck the top of the ceiling, did not go as high as the ceiling of the building but round about this cell. Anyone who knows anything would know that would probably be the result; and that was the finding. Listen to this:
(7)	In view of the evidence before them, Inspectors Craig and Dawson did not prepare an honest report for the minister,-
This is our royal commission, five years afterwards.
-hut rather sought to place the responsibility where it did not justly lie, on Buck, and this with a view to justifying the shooting, which they knew at the time to be unjustified.
I leave it >to the Minister of Justice whether he thinks that is a decent thing for any commission to say, in the light of the fact that Buck himself, when pressed for an answer, said that his speeches to the crowd would be calculated to instigate them to further effort. That is what he said; he was perfectly frank about it. Now we are told by this commission-and the reason is obvious-it all gets back to this poor unfortunate Dawson.
Let us go a step further:
(8)	The memorandum prepared by the superintendent for the Minister of Justice was prepared in an unwarranted effort to justify what had taken place, and the superintendent wrongfully omitted therein to report to the minister all the facts that were within his knowledge, or to give the minister an honest opinion in regard thereto.
I ask the right hon. Minister of Justice to-night as a fair man if he thinks that you can act on the recommendation of a commission which, five years after the event, makes a report like that with respect to these three men, Craig, Dawson and Ormond, under the circumstances mentioned. They charge them with being dishonest and deliberately making a dishonest report, and there are the marks of the shots. They are still there. They indicate the acute angle of fire. The reasons given at the hearing were clear and plain; and what is more, these men said that the effect of it was to do just what they wanted done, to quiet that riot. And listen to this: They say these men had no right to refer to what had taken place with respect to other cells where they had fired shots. But the answer was that the use of firearms had quieted the riot in the prison at cells E and F and that they used the same tactics with respect to the top tier D.
The issue is simple. Five years after the event, men who risked their lives, who were doing their duty as sworn officers of the law, are to be held up to ignominy; one of them, with a great record of offering his

life in the mud and muck of France and Flanders, is to be told that he is a dishonest man, without having an opportunity to defend himself except being called as I have stated, and questioned by three astute lawyers for eight days. Did he see the witnesses? Was he given an opportunity to see them? Did he hear them? He did not. The event took place in August, 1933, and now, in the summer of 1938, after five years, we have this announcement that Ormond made a dishonest report; that Craig and Dawson made a dishonest report.
Look at the report of Dawson. Dawson is the man that McRuer tried to crucify before Judge Daly and failed; now he has his chance and behind his back he puts it down in that record. That is the story, and on that we are asked to change the prison system of Canada. And it is so much the more intensified by the statement of the hon. member for Grey-Bruce this afternoon that he did not receive any pay. It was a vindictive act-

subtopic: INCORPORATION OF COMMISSION FOR ADMINISTRATION CONTROL AND MANAGEMENT-AMENDMENT OF EXISTING ACTS
speechtext: It was a generous act.

subtopic: INCORPORATION OF COMMISSION FOR ADMINISTRATION CONTROL AND MANAGEMENT-AMENDMENT OF EXISTING ACTS
speechtext:
-and we know what it was done for. Now he seizes the opportunity, paid by the people of this country, to make that report against the unfortunate Dawson whose only fault is that he did his duty.
Craig and Dawson signed a report on the Buck incident, and I must say it is a terrible thing to think that five years after we have this report being torn to pieces by these three men. Where were the witnesses? They were not concerned about them. Where were the militiamen? They were not concerned about them. Where were the guards? They were not concerned about them. It was condemnation. Listen to what Craig and Dawson did. These are the words:
1.	Close examination of the interior of cell 16-4-D, which is located on the fourth and top tier of D block, was made by the undersigned and it was found that there had been a bullet imbedded in the wall about six feet in height from the floor and two feet down from the ceiling, and approximately midway between the side walls, this mark (No. 1) was in the form of a round hole as deep as the forefinger. No. 2 bullet mark was in approximately the centre of the ceiling, a few inches to one side-this bullet had evidently ricochetted and had imbedded itself in the back wall, a little to one side of centre. No. 3, apparently, was the discharge of shotgun as ten marks as if made with shot, splattered on the back wall, were found around but mostly above No. 1 and No. 2 marks. No. 4 bullet mark was found on the iron bar of the *window directly in front of cell 16-4-D. These four bullet and shot marks were the only marks that could be found that would indicate firing on that part of the prison known as D block.

Penitentiaries Commission Act
Convict No. 2524, Timothy Buck, was confined in cell 16-4-D 'on October 20, 1932.

subtopic: INCORPORATION OF COMMISSION FOR ADMINISTRATION CONTROL AND MANAGEMENT-AMENDMENT OF EXISTING ACTS
speechtext: How many storeys?

subtopic: INCORPORATION OF COMMISSION FOR ADMINISTRATION CONTROL AND MANAGEMENT-AMENDMENT OF EXISTING ACTS
speechtext:
There were four tiers.
3.	The marks above mentioned prove conclusively that shots were fired into D block, three of them landing in Buck's cell, and one directly in front of the bar of the window.
I am reading from the report of the two inspectors made at the time.
4.	The evidence indicates that all these shots were fired between the hours of 5 p.m. and 8 p.m. Buck states that the firing started at 8 o'clock, other convicts state at an earlier time, but it is considered that the earlier hour is mentioned in an endeavour to show that it was light enough for them to recognize who did the shooting;
5.	None of the evidence taken gives information as to who actually did the shooting. One convict mentioned three officers' names but one of them was home sick on that day and the other two denied that they shot into D block, although at the time they state they were in that vicinity.
Has it come to this, that because men decline to act upon the evidence of convicts and to believe them when they had directed attention to three officers as having fired the shots, one of whom was at h_.me sick and the other two denied that they did it, five years afterwards three men on the strength of that say, "Dishonest Craig, dishonest Dawson and dishonest Ormond"?
This is very important in the light of what has occurred to-night:
6.	At about five o'clock that evening, it was ascertained that convicts in F block were digging through the partitions of their cells in an endeavour to congregate in the chapel and to effect an escape.
7.	The cells of F block were examined by the undersigned and it was found that holes had been dug in several cells, large enough for a man to crawl through.
8.	To prevent further digging and an escape, numerous shots were fired into the air and into the ceiling of F block; great noise and damage was going on in E block and a number of shots were fired similar to those into F block. These shots had the desired effect.
9.	Buck admits, and other evidence shows, that he made numerous speeches to the convicts that afternoon and evening. The nature of the speeches early in the afternoon may have been to quiet them hut it is evident, towards evening especially when the firing commenced into the other blocks, that he succeeded in working the convicts up by having them shout in unison to the troops to coerce them and also in chorus voicing their demands.
10.	This shouting by Buck was undoubtedly done at the gate of his cell in a gesticulatory manner and would be seen by the officers and militia patrolling and on duty in the yard. His actions and shouts would indicate clearly that he was leading and inciting the convicts.
11.	It is considered that the opinion was then formed by those on duty in the yard that action had to be taken to suppress Buck and the tumult he was the instigator of.
12.	The same action as taken with E and F blocks, was then evidently taken in regard to D block, by firing four or five shots high up in D block. These shots were fired at a moderately sharp angle from the yard but instead of hitting the ceiling as in the other blocks, entered cell 16 on the fourth or top^ tier of D block. The evidence shows these shots had the desired effect.
It has not been challenged, mark you, that these shots were fired at this sharp angle intc the ceiling; but owing to the fact that they were fired from the yard outside they fell short of the ceiling, as indicated by the report I have already read. But they had the desired effect. Now see the fairness of this report at the time:
13.	Whether aim was taken at Buck's cell, the evidence does not show, but it is apparent that from the high location of the marks those who fired the shots endeavoured to scare the convicts only, which evidently they did and the agitation was suppressed.
That is not denied. That is not questioned. These men risked their lives to suppress this commotion and quiet this agitation; yet, as a result of these efforts, five years later a commission calls them dishonest, and on the report of this commission we are asked to change the prison system of Canada.
Let us go a step further:
14.	It is the opinion of the undersigned that the shots fired into D block were not aimed deliberately at Buck or any other convict and that D block was treated similar to the other two blocks into which firing occurred.
Yet these three commissioners state: "The idea of Craig and Dawson mentioning these other blocks! What relevancy had they"? And Craig and Dawson point out why they did so. They point out that these men were getting out; that they were tearing down the walls; that they had already planned an escape into the chapel, and thence to freedom. I continue:
16.	It is pointed out that in the opinion of the undersigned, firing was the only reasonable means possible to suppress what was taking place at this stage. It was impossible at this time to take Buck out of his cell without precipitating a worse riot and possibly the loss of lives.
17.	It is the opinion of the undersigned that the firing into D block on the evening of October 20. 1932, was done by a member or members of the staff of the penitentiary or of the permanent militia, both of which were on duty in the vicinity from which the shots evidently came at that time.
18.	The undersigned are further of the opinion that the man or men when firing the shots
Penitentiaries Commission Act

into D block considered that they were fully justified in taking that action in the circumstances that then existed.
Respectfully submitted,
W. H. Craig,
Inspector.
J. D. Dawson,
Inspector.
Remember, this occurred six years ago next October. These men were on the spot. They were taking the responsibility. Their lives were being offered as a sacrifice, not the lives of these three commissioners. Yet the latter go to Kingston and hearken to stories, and they make a report that Dawson and Craig are dishonest men. Listen to these words:
The findings in the above report are subject to the following comments:
The references, in paragraphs 6, 7 and 8, to the nature of the disturbance in F and E blocks are irrelevant to the matter under consideration. Buck was in no way connected with any disturbances that may have taken place in these other cell blocks.
Just imagine; here were men with this terrible, this awful responsibility, with these hundreds of men in this penal institution, with this evidence that they had been burrowing their way into the open! They brought about quietness only by discharging firearms; then they suddenly saw the same situation in D tier, and they refer to that as a warrant for using the same means to bring about quiet there. Yet our beautiful commission says that is wholly irrelevant, and asks what that has to do with the matter.
Then I come to the next comment:
The finding in paragraph 9, that, "toward evening, especially when the firing into the other blocks commenced, he succeeded in working the convicts up, by having them shout in unison to the troops to coerce them, and also in chorus voicing their demands," is absurd.
Yet Buck has admitted it. That is your commission which is going to change the penal system of Canada. There you had these men confronted with that situation, as guardians of the peace, risking their lives, with the militia called out; and we are told that because they did what they did, as reported in this document by them at that time, it was all absurd, and that these men who risked their lives to preserve safety in that penitentiary were dishonest men. The report continues:
The troops were located outside the walls of the cell block. The prisoners were all locked in their cells. It is difficult to conceive how any shouting by Buck could have had the effect of "coercing" the armed troops in the yard. Careful perusal of the evidence does not justify such a conclusion.
The inferences drawn in paragraph 10 are unsupported by the evidence. The inspectors undertake to surmise what Buck would have done and what the officers might have seen, and on 
this basis they make the statement: "His actions and shouts would indicate clearly that he was leading and inciting the convicts." There is no evidence of such actions or shouts, and Inspector Dawson, when examined before the commission, expressed quite a different view from the above. He stated:
"I asked him (Buck) if his action might be interpreted as inciting rather than trying to quieten them, and he said 'Yes.' That more or less satisfied me on that point. This may be poor language."
The evidence Buck gave was as follows:
"Q. Is it possible that anyone in the distance would have thought that you were inciting rather than remonstrating?
A. Yes, it is possible owing to the noise and general excitement."
That is Buck's statement; yet in the face of that we have a report made six years later by three men who did not examine a single witness who was present at the time or who had anything to do with it, and in their report they make this finding against these men, charging them with dishonesty. Two of these men have worn the king's uniform and risked their lives in France and Flanders, but they are charged with being dishonest men. And that is the report upon which we are asked to change the penal system of Canada.
There is a rule of law, "False in one, false in all." Translated into ordinary English it just means that we should have an opportunity to study the evidence which should accompany the report. I propose, so far as it is possible to do so, to try to vindicate the position I take that we have a right to study this report. We are being asked to change our penal system on the report of men who ventured to make a report such as this regarding three men whom they charge with dishonesty one of whom they grilled for eight long days after having examined scores of convicts who gave evidence against him without his being given an opportunity either to see or hear them. I cannot do it.
Progress reported.
